because the subject and object are combined and designated as such, they are called the "ten Dharma-realms. These ten characters, when pronounced individually, signify the Dharma-realm, but when pronounced together, they convey the meaning of the "enabling cause" (*yuan-yin*).
Second, these ten kinds of dharmas have different boundaries and distinctions; cause and effect are separate, and there are differences between the ordinary and the sage.

Because they are distinct, the term "dhātu" (realm/element) is added to them; these ten dharmas together are called "dhātus," whereas calling them individually conveys the meaning of "pratyaya-hetu" (causal conditions).
Third, these ten are all subsumed within the *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm), which encompasses all phenomena. All phenomena tend toward hell; they do not exceed this tendency.
When their very substance is the principle itself, there is nothing further upon which to rely; therefore, it is named the *dharmadhātu*, and so on up to the Buddha.
The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is likewise so; the three characters [of this term] pronounced together signify the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*). Furthermore, it is said:
if the ten numbers rely upon the Dharma-realm, then that which relies follows what it relies upon and thus enters the realm of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dhātu*).

The separation of the boundaries of the ten realms is the realm of the provisional (*prajñapti-dhātu*). That all ten numbers rely upon the Dharma-realm is the realm of the Middle (*madhyama-dhātu*). This is intended to...
The interpretation of the *Yì* (Book of Changes) is thus: by discerning the meaning as it is intended, one speaks of emptiness, which is precisely the provisional and the middle;
there is no one, two, or three, yet there are one, two, and three, as previously stated (*etc.*). △ Second, regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*: first, citing and pointing to the scriptural text.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not transcend the provisional and the real.
Second, the conclusion establishes the three causes:

all phenomena are the "provisional" within the context of the same essence; the conditions and the consummation (*pratyaya* and *niṣyanda*), as well as the true reality, are the "real" within the context of the same essence. Both of these encompass both good and evil.
The nine realms and ten suchnesses as the direct cause are the evil conditions; the Buddha realm and ten suchnesses are the good conditions.
Reading this three times, one realizes that the direct cause is complete and lacking nothing.

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the *Lotus Sūtra* does not transcend the provisional and the real, and the provisional and the real do not transcend the ten realms, which possess both horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Regarding these two treatises, if one discusses them from a vertical perspective, the Buddha-realm is the real and the nine realms are provisional;

yet when speaking of their mutual inclusion, the mutual inclusion of the Buddha-fruit within the nine realms is the real, while the mutual inclusion of the nine realms within the Buddha-realm is the provisional.

As the Great Master said: "If discussed in detail, each possesses both the provisional and the real"—this is precisely what is meant. From a horizontal perspective, each of the ten realms possesses [all others].
The three causes—the direct cause and the two conditions—belong to the Real (the ultimate), while the two conditions belong to the Provisional (the expedient).

When the direct cause is taken as the conditions, it is Real yet Provisional; when the conditions are taken as the direct cause, they are Provisional yet Real. Thus, the ten realms coexist within a single nature;

how could the provisional and the real be divided like the distance between Yan and Yue? All phenomena are of one substance; within this provisional unity, there are good and evil, as well as the direct and conditional causes.

This is discussed in terms of all phenomena (*dharmas*) belonging to the provisional and the real; yet, apart from all phenomena, there is no separate real aspect—what is provisional that is not real?
Apart from the real aspect, there are no phenomena—what is real that is not provisional? The identity of the provisional and the real is perfectly exhausted therein.
To speak of the nine realms and the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) is to mean that even evil conditions serve as the cause for the third [stage].
Having finished reading this, it is indeed complete and without omission; these are the passages from the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) that explain the phenomena of sentient beings.

First, it cites a sutra, saying: "That which is called all dharmas have such characteristics, such natures, such essences, such powers, such functions, such causes, such conditions, such fruits, and such retributions—such is their original state."
Regarding the phrase "Ultimate Equality" (*mo jiujing deng*), Master Tiantai stated that reading the text according to its meaning involves three shifts: first, "This mark is suchness;
this nature is suchness," and so on, up to "this retribution is suchness"; second, "Such is the mark, such is the nature," and so on, up to "such is the retribution";
third, "The mark is suchness, the nature is suchness," and so on, up to "the retribution is suchness. If all [of these]...
To say that "suchness" (tathatā) is not different from its name is the meaning of emptiness (śūnyatā).

To speak of such characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and such nature (svabhāva) is to point to the provisional designations (prajñapti) of names for the characteristics and nature of emptiness, which differ according to their gradual distinctions; this is the meaning of the conventional (saṃvṛti).
To speak of such characteristics and such nature as being "thus" within the reality of the Middle Way is the meaning of the middle (madhyama).
To facilitate understanding through analysis, the emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are clarified; by grasping their meaning, one speaks of them as such.
When clarifying emptiness, "one emptiness is all emptiness"; when pointing to the provisional, "one provisional is all provisional";
and according to this, "one middle is all middle. These are not one, two, or three, yet they manifest as one, two, and three—neither vertical nor horizontal.
This is called the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively realize this Dharma. These ten dharmas encompass all dharmas.
Depending on the meaning, they may be analyzed into three aspects; depending on the recitation, one should follow the verse text, which says:
"Such great fruits and rewards, with their various natures and characteristics," and so forth. Thus, the ten realms are combined and separated through three modes of recitation.

The text [records] how the masters and disciples of Nanyue and Tiantai have transmitted this lineage; their ingenious insights beyond the literal words all involve roaming the mind within the *bhūtatathatā* (true reality), rather than being concerned with scholastic exegesis.
They are like Cook Ding, who in dissecting oxen has advanced beyond mere skill, seeing no whole ox before his eyes.
△ Third, regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Part One: Briefly Indicating the Meaning of the Scripture.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is taught that both icchantikas and virtuous persons possess both innate goodness and innate evil, which are termed the "causes and conditions for good and evil.
The wording and meaning cited here are both abbreviated; were they to be presented in full, one should cite the thirty-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Second, it is said that there may be a Buddha-nature present in icchantikas but absent in those with roots of goodness;
or a Buddha-nature present in those with roots of goodness but absent in icchantikas; or a Buddha-nature present in both types of persons; or a Buddha-nature absent in both types of persons.
Regarding the first two phrases, they refer to the Buddha-nature as the cultivated *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause) for defilement and the cultivated *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) for evil.
This is the nature [of Buddha-nature]. For the Buddha has severed and cultivated away all defiled cultivation and evil cultivation, and has fulfilled pure cultivation and wholesome cultivation;

therefore, these [aspects of] defiled and evil cultivation do not exist in the Buddha’s nature or his roots of goodness. The next two phrases refer to the Buddha-nature as the *nirvedhabhāga* (the cause of realization through cultivation) and the *pratyaya-hetu* (the causal condition of wholesome cultivation).
This is because the icchantika has severed and exhausted all pure cultivation and wholesome cultivation, and cultivates only defilement.

Because they have fulfilled their cultivation of evil, this Buddha-nature is absent in icchantikas. The two phrases concerning the third and second [categories] refer to the Buddha-nature of the fundamental cause (正因佛性), which encompasses both innate goodness and innate evil.
For although a Buddha has severed all defiled cultivation and exhausted all cultivated evil, he does not sever his innate defilement or innate evil;
likewise, although an icchantika has severed all pure cultivation and exhausted all cultivated goodness, he does not sever his innate purity or innate goodness.

Because the Icchantika does not sever the nature of purity and the nature of goodness, yet possesses the nature of defilement and the nature of evil, they attain mastery over evil upon reaching the stage of fruition;
thus, they extensively employ the dharma-gate of the "nature of evil" to transform and deliver sentient beings.

Because the Icchantika does not sever the nature of purity and the nature of goodness, at a later time they again give rise to the cultivation of purity and the cultivation of goodness as antidotes to the cultivation of defilement and the cultivation of evil. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its latter section, speaks of the Icchantika.

The attainment of Buddhahood by the *icchantika* is fundamentally based on this. The two lines concerning the fourth and second [categories] state that there is yet another Buddha-nature which both types of persons lack;
this refers to the nature of non-retrogression. △ Second, the conclusion establishing the three causes: 1. The formal conclusion.

Since the three causes are wondrous, speech must necessarily possess the conditions for understanding; correct understanding must necessarily possess correct conditions; and correct speech must necessarily possess both conditions and understanding.

Understanding must necessarily possess these three, and the three are identical to the one. Do not cling to the literal words and thereby harm the perfection [of the teaching], nor misrepresent the intent of the Sage.
△ Second, the mutual integration.

If this is so, since the nine realms possess the nature of the three causes—defilement as the *jñānahetu* (revealing cause), evil as the *pratyayahetu* (conditioning cause), and non-duality of defilement and evil as the *hetuhetu* (causal cause)—how could the causal cause of evil be restricted solely to the Buddha-realm?
Furthermore, since the three causes are by nature good, the conditioning cause is pure, and the revealing cause is both good and pure.
Non-duality is precisely the correct primary cause (*samyag-hetu*).

People today know only that by contemplating the true, eternal, and pure consciousness one cultivates the correct primary cause for the Buddha-realm; this is what is called "contemplating only the pure *tathatā*.
This is precisely because they do not understand that [the mind] possesses the three causes for all nine realms. Since our school has already revealed these...
When the Mahāyāna clearly reveals this, one may cultivate all ten realms and the three causes;

however, one should observe and cultivate them according to whichever realm manifests before one, returning to and restoring [the source]. It is not necessary to abandon the waves to seek the water, nor to discard emptiness to seek emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that if this were so, it would not only be refuted by the critique of mere words, but would also cause...
While these words refer to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), their scope is limited to the three causes within the Buddha-realm;

yet, if one were to further deny them, people today know only the "understanding cause" (liǎoyīn) for cultivating the Buddha-realm, because they take only the single emptiness as their primary principle.
Not only do they fail to cultivate the "correct cause" (zhèngyīn) of the Middle Way, they do not even understand the "conditional cause" (yuányīn) of the conventional truth.
This is because Xiu abandoned numerous worldly matters and esteemed principle. △ Fourth, following the indication, there are two parts. First, a general reference to various sutras:

This nature, whether good or evil, is also called the pure nature or the defiled nature; it is also called the luminous principle or the dark principle; it is also called the permanent or the non-existent.
The essence of eternal dual quiescence.
△ Second, citing the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*:

as in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, the term "poisonous harm" (*du-hai*) may be used alone; this "poisonous harm" is precisely the nature of evil (*xing-è*), both being alternative names for the single essence.
Furthermore,
regarding the invocation of Avalokiteśvara or the single name "Subduer of Poisonous Harm" (*Duhai*), the meaning of the cited scriptural passages is here abbreviated;
for a full citation of Master Tiantai’s commentary on the *Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī for Subduing Poisonous Harm*, please refer to that source.
The *Nī-sūtra* states: "This sūtra is titled according to both person and dharma. 'Person' is the supreme designation for Great Compassion; 'dharma' is the divine mantra of the Most Holy.
Regarding 'person,' there are two meanings: general and specific. The specific is the eminent name of Avalokiteśvara; the general is the auspicious title of a Bodhisattva.
The specific further has two meanings: first, the agent; second, the object. This refers to the character 'to request' (*qing*)."
These three characters, "Avalokiteśvara," designate the Sage Lord who is capable of responding; they signify the various capacities [of sentient beings] that can be moved [by his response].

There are two meanings to this Dharma: first, its function (*vṛtti*), and second, its essence (*svabhāva*). "Extinguishing and subduing poisonous harms" clarifies its power and function, while the *dhāraṇī* clarifies its true essence.
Regarding the essence, there are two meanings: in this context, it is called "that which can obstruct and sustain," sustaining the three [realms].

The meaning of "obstructing" refers to the function of warding off two extremes, which are categorized as three: first, the object; second, the practice; and third, the principle. The "object" refers to tigers, wolves, swords, blades, and the like.
The "practice" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five stages of dwelling. The "principle" refers to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is unimpeded and untainted;
yet that which is tainted is the poison within the nature of reality. Therefore, it is said that the name is designated based on both persons and dharmas. — *Gushan* (Gushan Zhiyuan).

The *Fashichanyichao* (Explanatory Notes on the Meaning of the Dharma) states: "The unobstructed nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) refers to the three truths as one mind; this is called the dharma-realm.

Because the Buddhas and sentient beings are mutually fused and each and every thing is omnipresent, it is said to be 'unobstructed. Regarding 'being unstained yet stained,' the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* says:
'The self-nature of the middle way, the pure mind, is not defiled by afflictions; it is fundamentally neither bound nor liberated.'"
That which is unstained yet appears stained is difficult to comprehend; this refers to sentient beings who, deluded regarding their true nature, give rise to the sixty-two views.

Examining the meaning of those words, they accord well with the present text. If one were to interpret the present text [according to other systems], it would have to be said that the *dharmatā* and ignorance together universally produce all phenomena;
thus, while remaining unstained, it becomes stained, and the entire rational nature (*li-xing*) becomes poison—this is what is called [the state of being stained].
The poison of principle (*tarkaviṣa*) is so called because it is a poison of principle; thus, there is also the poison of practice and the poison of phenomena.
Now, observing that all dharmas are but the mind, their defiled substance is entirely pure; this is the governance of the poison of principle through divine mantras.

Consequently, the subsequent passages of the sutra all enter into the realm of suchness (*yathābhūta*). Nevertheless, although the commentary of Gushan elucidates this, it remains obscure, for it ultimately results in harm.

If the meaning of the inherent evil of nature (*prakṛti-pāpa*) is not clarified, it would be better to cite the Great Master’s commentary on the subsequent passage for a correct interpretation, which explains the *dhāraṇī* for "subduing and eliminating poisonous harm" as follows:
"Eliminate" (*xiao*) means to remove; "subdue" (*fu*) means to tame. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Eliminate the three obstructions so that there are no evils;
the five eyes are fully perfected, and one attains Bodhi. This merely removes the illness, but does not remove the dharma.
For example, although a venomous snake possesses poison, one merely eliminates its sting so that it does not harm people, yet one need not kill it.
By subduing the poison of the three obstacles and making them amenable to being ridden, they become gateways for entering the Path;
according to their capacity for deliverance, they are liberated. Therefore, there is no need to sever them, as will also be explained below regarding non-severance.

This is clear evidence that while there is severing, it is not a severing [of the nature of reality]. △ Second, the difference between the extensive and the concise, in four parts: First, pointing out the numbers of the extensive and concise.
Regarding the difference between the extensive and concise according to the sharpness or dullness of faculties: the concise consists of ten realms, while the extensive consists of thirty.
Briefly stated, the text on the ten realms appears in the *Avataṃsaka*, where they are divided into ten dharma-realms according to the conditions of defilement or purity;
extensively stated, the three thousandfold world is a principle that ultimately returns to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*’s true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Someone may ask:

"The *Avataṃsaka* consists of only half a verse, yet it is called 'brief,' while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* consists of four lines, yet it is called 'extensive. Why is this? The answer is: Although the *Avataṃsaka* is but half [a verse],...
In the verse, it is merely named the "Ten Realms," and although the *Lotus Sūtra* consists of four-character lines, its meaning encompasses the "Ten Suchnesses.
Master Tiantai then combined the extensive and the concise, expanding upon them to establish the principle of the "Hundred Realms and Thousand Suchnesses" and the "Three Thousand Nature-Phenomena.
Only through this can the intent of the *Avataṃsaka*’s Dharma-realm and the tenet of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s True Reality be fully realized.
Thus, the essence of the principle-body of sentient beings as realized by the Tathāgata—the substance of cause and effect and the nature of cultivation—is likewise fully exhausted herein.
The meaning of its pervasive expansion is detailed in the following text. △ Second, clarifying the substance of the extensive and the concise.
Thus we know that good and evil do not transcend the ten realms; the natures of these ten realms are fused and mutually inclusive, forming one hundred realms.
Since each realm possesses the ten suchnesses, they form one thousand suchnesses. These consist of one thousand provisional names, one thousand five aggregates, and one thousand lands.
The principle that good and evil do not transcend the ten realms will be clarified in the following text;

for now, I shall clarify the meaning of the two sutras following the same track to demonstrate that the nature is replete with the three thousand [realms]. First, according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the ten realms are fused to become one hundred realms;

thus it is said that the natures of the ten realms are fused and mutually inclusive, forming the hundred dharma-realms. Next, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the ten suchnesses are fused.

Because there are one thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*), they are called "realms" (*dhātu*); ten suchnesses thus constitute one thousand suchnesses. Furthermore, next, according to the *Renyō-kyō* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra), the three dharmas are fused with the hundred realms and one thousand suchnesses to become the "three thousand," hence it is said: "one thousand provisional names, one thousand five aggregates (*skandha*), and one thousand lands.
Moreover, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, within the commentary on the one hundred and eight samādhis, up to the explanation of "that which can illuminate one... [the same principle is applied].

Regarding the *Sarvalokadhātu-samādhi*: because one attains this samādhi, one is able to illuminate the three kinds of worlds—namely, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of their dwelling places (*sthāna-loka*), and the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*). The Great Master of the Four Vidyās stated:

"Therefore, our school employs the meaning of that treatise's 'three periods' to expound the Dharma Flower; its wondrous discourse on the ten suchnesses [of the *Daśabhūmika*] certainly does not merely refer to the ordinary."
This is what the heart aspires to attain. △ Third, the summary of the essential point of the one mind:
Thus, the three thousand [realms] are inherently complete within the present single thought-moment of the mind that cultivates evil.

Regarding the statement that "a single thought-moment of cultivated evil is fully endowed with the three thousand [realms]," this refers merely to the fact that when a single thought arises through the mutual correspondence of sense organs and objects, it necessarily belongs to one realm;

since each realm is mutually endowed with the others, they constitute the hundred realms and the three thousand realms. However, if one discusses the actual essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is truly more than this.
Someone might raise an objection: "Now, the Master Zhiyi, based on the translation from the Qin dynasty, has clearly elucidated the ten suchnesses."
Therefore, one may discuss the three thousand [worlds]. If it is asked: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated during the Western Jin dynasty lists only six aspects;
where, then, is the meaning of the three thousand? The answer is: "In our current discussion of the inherent nature (*xingju*), we clarify only the ontological essence (*liti*).
As for the number of items, it can certainly be calculated; following the six aspects, we designate them as the 'one thousand' of the inherent nature."

What is so wrong with eight hundred [verses]? Furthermore, although there may be additions or omissions in a translation depending on the meaning, the essential meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* realm remains ultimately unimpaired.
Moreover, as for the original meaning of the Jin translation, it was not exhaustive; how can one rely upon it when it was subject to the personal preferences of the translators?
The Qin translation has been widely propagated and stands out prominently; if it were not for this, and the Jin translation remained obscure and untransmitted, would that not be the case?
"It is without cause" (and so forth). △ Fourth, manifesting the subtle, wondrous, and pervasive interpenetration:
it is not accomplished through fabrication, nor does it arise through mutual production, nor does it exist through mutual conjunction.

A single thought-moment does not precede the three thousand [realms], and the three thousand do not follow after the single thought-moment. The single thought-moment is no less, and the three thousand are no more.

Because this is the wondrous realm of non-action, it is not a product of conditioned creation; because all phenomena are fundamentally inherent, they are not produced through the arising of characteristics;
because characteristics are perfectly manifest, they do not contain one another. The three thousand realms are identical to a single thought-moment;

the single thought-moment does not precede them, for the single thought-moment is itself the three thousand realms; the three thousand realms do not follow after it, for the single thought-moment fully possesses the three thousand realms and thus is never deficient.

Because the three thousand worlds reside within a single thought-moment, the three thousand are not many. △ Second, clarifying the characteristics of the contemplation of the truths (di-guan), in six parts:
first, clarifying the reason for establishing the truths and practicing correct contemplation; second, clarifying that one destroys deluded attachments but does not destroy phenomena.
One must know that while the mind can be broken, the Dharma cannot be broken; yet the attachment to dharmas becomes a sickness and must also be broken.
These words serve both to resolve doubts and to reveal the profound mystery. Someone might ask:

"If cultivating evil is itself the nature of evil, why is it necessary to establish the three contemplations to break the three delusions? The answer is: "The contemplations break the delusions; [it is not that the nature of evil is broken]."
It is the emotions that obstruct the Dharma; emotion is deluded emotion, and delusion is the three afflictions.
This deluded emotion has existed for a long time, beginning from fundamental ignorance and continuing until the final thought-moment of Equal Enlightenment.

Since the essential principle is inherently subtle while emotional attachment regards it as coarse, those who destroy delusions merely destroy the emotions regarding the three thousand [realms], but do not destroy the three thousand [realms] themselves.

Regarding this Dharma, the present-day schools do not follow it, instead following deluded sentiments; they merely manifest that all dharmas are inherently complete, for every dharma is a wondrous mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and every mark is real.

Thus, the title calls it the "Wondrous Dharma" (*Myōhō*), and the Sūtra speaks of "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); there is indeed a profound reason for this. To resolve doubts and reveal the wondrous lies precisely in this.
However, there are those who take the medicine and turn it into a disease, failing to find the proper method for practicing the threefold contemplation (*santivaśa*).
On the contrary, to turn this into the three delusions would require further application of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to dismantle them; that is not the intent here.

What is meant by "clinging to phenomena becomes an affliction" is as follows: one clings to the fact that cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*), and thus extensively practices cultivated evil through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This is what is called "grasping a snake without restraint. Such cultivated evil must precisely be destroyed. △
Second, it clarifies that the fundamental essence of principle (*li-ti*) cannot be severed.
Thus, good and evil, purity and defilement, are all gateways to the Dharma; the essence of this principle is fundamentally luminous and pure, not severing even the slightest trace.

Following the previous passage which stated that while emotion (*qing*) may be destroyed, the Dharma cannot be destroyed, is it not the case that good and evil, purity and defilement, are [all such gateways]?
The principle-body of the Dharma-gate is, by its very nature, originally luminous and pure; at the time of attaining Buddhahood, not even a hair’s breadth of it is severed.
△ Third, clarifying delusion and awakening through the lens of defilement and purity:
thus, the categories of severance and realization, as well as delusion and awakening, are discussed solely in terms of defilement and purity.

Some may doubt this, asking: "If the essence is already luminous and pure, without even a hair’s breadth of interruption, why does the sutra further speak of severance and realization, or delusion and awakening?
Therefore, the commentary explains: "Thus, severance, realization, delusion, and awakening are discussed solely in terms of defilement and purity.

This refers to what is called in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* the "ten dharma-realms according to their respective portions," which follow along with conditions of either defilement or purity. Following conditions of defilement...
When defiled by defiling conditions, it constitutes the nine realms; when purified by purifying conditions, it constitutes the Buddha-dharma realm.
△ Fourth, refuting the ancients' lack of the eye of discernment regarding dharmas.

Those of the past lacked the Dharma-eye that discriminates between principle and phenomena; they failed to distinguish between medicine and disease, and as soon as they heard it said in the air that "one mark is negated" and "not established," they immediately interpreted this as nihilistic annihilation.

They took the provisional contemplation (*jia-guan*)—which names the illumination of the three thousand worlds—to be a fixed doctrine asserting that the three thousand worlds are established as real dharmas.
If the Three Truths merely negate, how could there be any establishment of dharmas?
Emotion is delusion, while principle is the fundamental substance. Deluded emotion constitutes a sickness that should be eradicated by the medicine of the Dharma.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs established this medicine by relying internally on principle to establish the wisdom of the three contemplations based on the objects of the Three Truths;
they also established it by relying externally on the sickness to apply the wisdom of the three contemplations based on the three types of delusion. This, then, is the medicine.

Although there is a principle of provisional shifting between these [phenomena] and illness, the substance of their nature remains entirely unchanged; yet people of the past did not understand this meaning.
Hearing that the three contemplations of Tiantai "negate" existence, they took this to mean negating the extremes and interpreted it as nihilistic annihilation;

hearing that [the teaching of] "provisional establishment" illuminates existence, they dogmatically asserted that the three thousand dharmas are established as real entities. This is to be deluded by names and fail to know the truth.
This is the meaning. Now, let us reverse the question: each of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) is distinguished by its aspect of negation (*vighāta*) and illumination (*āloka*).

If one were to interpret it in this way, even if one were to crudely distinguish between the manifest and the subtle, if there were negation within them, then the principle that all three truths are simultaneously negated would follow;

not only would the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) be simultaneously negated, but emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) would likewise be simultaneously negated. How, then, could one establish the [positive] dharmas? If one were to apply the same logic to establish illumination, then [the same fault would apply to all three].
If both truths are illuminated together, then it is not merely the conventional truth and the two extremes that are illuminated; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is also illuminated.
How, then, could there be annihilation? △ Fifth, explaining the application of contemplation to dispel delusion.

Because deluded passions must be shattered, one employs the principle that they are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle. Upon realizing this, the single thought-moment of a mind engaged in cultivated evil is itself the wondrous realm of the three thousand [realms].
Building upon the previous chapter, while deluded passions may be shattered, phenomena cannot be shattered; because phenomena cannot be shattered, their essence is fundamentally luminous and pure.

Not a single hair’s breadth of this [delusion] is severed, for it is difficult to eliminate such deluded sentiments; therefore, one should employ the three contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way to break through them.
Although it is said that they are "broken," in reality there is no other method to break them;

it is simply by means of these three contemplations that one realizes this single thought—the mind arising in conjunction with the faculties and objects—as the wondrous realm of the three thousand [dharmas]. Thus, the three truths and the three contemplations are cultivated.
Thus, the identity between [phenomena] and nature is established spontaneously. △ Sixth, clarifying that because afflictions are shattered, the Dharma is revealed:

Since cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil, it is the principle of the three thousand [realms] as they are inherently possessed; yet this cultivated evil is precisely the wondrous reality of the three thousand.
If cultivated evil were simply evil, then while the good would be subtle and wondrous, the evil would be coarse; thus, one would have to overturn and destroy it.
Now, since cultivated evil is precisely inherent evil (xing-è), this cultivated evil is the three thousand realms as they are inherently possessed within reality (li-jù sānqiān).
It is the secret treasury of the three virtues—Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti—which is perfected in its very essence. Is this cultivated evil, then, not itself a wondrous matter?
For these three reasons, the Great Master clarified that the principle-nature (*riji*) of all beings is Buddha. He stated: "This is the Perfect Wisdom and Perfect Enlightenment;
all dharmas pervade all places, and there is nothing that is not clearly understood. This means that inherent evil (*shōaku*) is itself the Dharma-body (*hosshin*). Furthermore, he said:
"Even though one commits the five heinous crimes (*gogyon*), they are all the aspect of liberation. This means that cultivated evil (*shūaku*) is itself liberation. Moreover—
"Though clouds may obscure and delude one’s vision, the principle remains. This means that the cultivation of defilement is itself *prajñā*. Therefore, it is said:
"This is precisely the wondrous reality of the three thousand [realms]. △ Seventh, clarifying how the contemplation of principle can encompass phenomena.

One simply contemplates the principle (li), wherein both the negation and establishment of the three thousand [realms] are simultaneously achieved; these are naturally subsumed within the dharma-realm as the functioning of the three thousand phenomena (shi-yong).

Someone may ask: "The fruition of the Buddhas' realization possesses the three thousand phenomena as actual functioning; if one now merely contemplates cultivation as identical to nature, what becomes of that actual functioning?
In response, it is said: "By merely contemplating the three thousand as inherent in the principle, one skillfully employs the three contemplations (*sanguan*), using emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to..."
The three delusions are simultaneously shattered by means of the Provisional (jia), and the Three Truths are simultaneously established by means of the Middle (zhong).
Thus, the principle that "delusion is itself truth" constitutes the function of equal contemplation within the Dharma-realm; once this is perfected, it will manifest of its own accord before long.
What need is there to worry about the phenomenal functions of the three thousand realms at the stage of fruition? △ Eighth, clarifying the mutual integration of principle and phenomena.

The three thousand [realms] are all the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); their characteristics are perfectly manifest, for phenomena and principle are fundamentally fused, not being a mere enumeration of dharmas.
The Sūtra says, "the true aspect of all dharmas"; "all dharmas" refers to the three thousand phenomena, while "true aspect" refers to the principle of *tathatā*.
When the true aspect is identical with all dharmas, then principle is identical with phenomena; when all dharmas are identical with the true aspect, then phenomena are identical with principle.
When phenomena are identical to principle, then the three thousand realms are all reality; when principle is identical to phenomena, then their characteristics appear vividly.

Is it not the case that phenomenon and principle are fundamentally fused in essence? How could this be compared to the worldly method of counting heads, where "this" and "that" are separated and the one and the many are not integrated?
As the text below states: "All things are identical to a single place, and thus they can be the same."
Because they abide in the unification of a single thought-moment, it is like many pearls all tending toward one [string]; this is what is meant by that.
△ Ninth, clarifying that this reveals what is not to be negated:
since it does not belong to that which is to be negated, how could it not be that which is revealed?

This means that although one employs the three contemplations to shatter deluded sentiments, while the sentiments are eliminated, the principle is revealed; the elimination of sentiments is not what is being destroyed, whereas the revelation of the principle is what is established.
Does not the Great Master say: "For example, in the case of a venomous snake, if only its poison is neutralized without its life being extinguished, it can still be ridden;
how much more so the case of a stinging wasp? 10. Concluding the Formation of the Nature of Evil within Nirvana.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas do not sever their inherent evil, and the icchantikas do not sever their inherent good. By pointing to this single principle, all obstructions naturally dissolve.

To point to this single principle means that the three thousand [realms] are all the true aspect (*dharmatā*); their characteristics are manifest and complete, and since they do not belong to that which is to be destroyed, how could they not be so?

It is not that which is manifested; rather, it is because these three thousand [realms] are all the true aspect (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), their characteristics being perfectly present within phenomenal functions.

Regarding the three thousand as phenomenal functions, only Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively investigate the true aspect of all phenomena; thus, how could the inherent evil of the nine realms ever be severed?
Regarding the three thousand as the principle-endowment (*li-jù*), all sentient beings are primordially Buddhas, yet the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm remains distinct.
How could it ever be that [the teachings] were severed? It is for this reason that Tiantai took the *Lotus Sūtra* as his ultimate refuge and deeply realized the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
indeed, these two meanings encompass the essential purport of the Great Doctrine. △ Eleven: Citing Questions and Answers to Elucidate the Three [Points].
First, clarifying that the Buddha merely severed the good and evil of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Question: What kind of good and evil do icchantikas and Buddhas sever? Answer: Icchantikas sever all cultivated good and fulfill all cultivated evil;
Buddhas sever all cultivated evil and fulfill all cultivated good.
The text for the questions and answers herein is derived from the *Guanyin Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara). Master Huxi has briefly cited it to clarify its meaning;

it is not necessarily identical to that work, and students need only know its general outline. △ Second, clarifying that the wondrousness of cultivating good and evil does not belong to that which is refuted.

Question: Since the cultivation of good and the cultivation of evil are both wondrous matters, they belong to that which is manifested (*prabhāvya*). Why, then, are they called that which is to be destroyed (*bādhyam*)? Answer:
The cultivation of good and evil is identical to the nature of good and evil; there is no cultivation of good or evil to be discussed. This is the meaning of "severance" (*prahāṇa*);

therefore, the Buddhas have severed all cultivated evil to its end, and the icchantikas have severed all cultivated good to its end. Since the cultivation of good and evil is identical to the nature of good and evil, what [cultivation of good and evil] could there be?
"Once one has severed this meaning of 'not severing,' the subtlety of both severance and non-severance lies therein.
In the response, the most essential point is that when practicing good or evil, they are themselves the nature of good or evil; there is no "practiced" good or evil to be discussed.
This is the meaning of "severance. For if there were practiced good or evil to be discussed, it would mean one does not understand the meaning of "immediacy" (ji).

If one does not know that cultivation is identical to nature, then the contentious debates between the "good" and "evil" schools of Wu and Chu will remain in disarray; this is simply because the principle of decisive judgment has not been grasped.

It is precisely because one fully understands that the cultivation of good and evil is already identical to the nature of good and evil, that the cultivation of good and evil has never needed to be severed from that identity.

Since it is not severed, yet one acts as if there were a severance—this is why the subtlety lies within. Fearing that later students might not yet have awakened to this, [the Master] again established two [distinctions].
Regarding the first point of clarifying the phrases: first, one must realize that there is no distinction between cultivation and nature;

second, one must realize that there is no difference between good and evil—meaning that where there is no cultivation, good and evil can be discussed. △ Third, clarifying whether the Buddhas of the Three Periods sever or do not sever good and evil, and whether they are the same or different.
Question: Do icchantikas, who do not sever inherent goodness, give rise to cultivated goodness; and do the Buddhas, who do not sever inherent evil, likewise give rise to cultivated evil?
Answer: Because icchantikas do not realize inherent goodness and are defiled by [the notion of] goodness, they give rise to cultivated goodness, which extensively treats all evils.
Because the Buddhas are able to realize evil, they possess mastery over evil, and thus evil no longer arises; instead, they extensively employ all [phenomena].

The wondrous function of transforming sentient beings through evil is called the "Dharma-gate of Evil" because it is untainted; although it lacks the marks of defilement or obstruction, it possesses the marks of inherent nature.
Within the true suchness and wondrous nature of all Buddhas and sentient beings, the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses are primordially and fully present.

It is like a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel; being capable of both good and evil, he is said to be "unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanged.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Because it can follow defiled or pure conditions, it consequently divides into the ten dharma-realms.

When sentient beings are deluded and follow defiled conditions to create the nine realms, the Buddha-realm remains hidden while the nine realms manifest; thus, the function of defilement accords with their minds.

Yet its wondrous function is not manifest; though it is said to be unmanifest, the Buddha-nature is majestic and has never failed to appear, but sentient beings are themselves deluded and pass it by right before their faces.
When the Buddhas awaken and, following pure conditions, create the Buddha-realm, then the Buddha-realm manifests while the nine realms recede;
yet though the nine realms are said to recede, the essential nature of the nine realms is fundamentally identical.
When [the Buddha] is in a state of quiescence, his activities are withdrawn and he abides in mastery; thus, while the Buddha is manifest, the nine realms are hidden.
When he manifests his activity, however, he proceeds through the ten realms, and all are clearly revealed. Therefore it is said:

"Those who should be saved by a Buddha-body, for them he immediately manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma; those who should be saved by the bodies of the nine realms, for them he likewise [manifests those bodies]."

To manifest these forms and preach the Dharma for them is called the "Universal Gate Manifestation" (*samantamukha-prakāśana*); it is precisely here that one attains actual realization. Therefore, it is said:
"Extensively employing all manner of evil to transform and deliver sentient beings; its wondrous function is untainted, thus it is named the 'Gate of Evil Dharmas'.

Because these acts are performed out of necessity rather than choice, they are nominally designated as "evil"; consequently, while they possess the appearance of delusion, they inherently possess their true nature.

The application of these [six roots]. △ Twelfth, judging the stages according to the six identities (liu ji): First, the Dharma. At the level of ordinary beings (bo di), there is only the principle (li) and the name;
at the initial hearing, the contemplative practice (guan xing) has not yet manifested or been verified. The essence remains obscured, though the six faculties (liu gen) appear to have awakened.
At the first stage (chu zhu), partial vision is attained; at the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment (miao jue guo cheng jiu jing), it becomes clearly manifest.

Ordinary people possess only principle, and this principle is precisely the three thousand [realms]. Regarding the term "name" (*mingzi*): when one first hears that the nature is replete with the ten realms, it is called "knowing that the nature is replete with the three thousand.

Regarding the term "character" (*zi*): although the wisdom of the three contemplations has not yet been manifested in the stage of contemplative practice (*guangxing*), one contemplates the objects of the three thousand realms;
yet, because the delusions of the five abodes have not been shattered despite being suppressed, one verifies that the substance of the three thousand remains obscured by confusion and unmanifest.

The stage of "resemblance" (*sādharmya*) involves the manifestation of the three thousand [realms] through the arousal of a semblance of breaking the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), thereby attaining the purity of the six sense organs.

At the first *bhūmi*, there is partial realization of the true; from here up to the *saṃbodhi* (Equal Enlightenment), one partially breaks through ignorance (*avidyā*) and partially realizes the three thousand.
When the fruit of *miao-jue* (Wondrous Enlightenment) is accomplished, it is ultimately and clearly manifest. Only Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively fathom these three thousand realms.
The Dharma is the true reality (*dharmatā*). △ Second, the two analogies: first, the analogy of the three men.

This means that the principle must be personally realized for its characteristics to become manifest; it is like when Lord Cao [Cao Cao] was hidden, his features were revealed only after he removed his clothes. The matter can be understood by comparison:
it is like when Sun [Quan] and Liu [Biao] were manifest, they were clearly visible before one's eyes.
Formerly, at the end of the Han dynasty, Liu, Sun, and Cao—these three men—went together to consult a physiognomist.

The physiognomist first predicted that the positions of both Sun and Liu would reach the level of Son of Heaven, while alone Cao Gong did not receive such approval. Thereupon, Cao Gong removed his robe to show himself to the physiognomist, who, upon seeing him, let out a loud cry and wept bitterly, saying:
"From this point on, the world will be in turmoil and the cauldron will boil over. Subsequently, this indeed came to pass extensively.
Each of these rulers claimed supremacy over their respective regions and styled themselves emperors; at that time, some people detested both men and gave them these designations:
Cao Cao was called a "treacherous hero" (jiānxióng) and Liu Bei a "fierce hero" (xiāoxióng).

While Cao Cao’s being a treacherous hero is indeed accurate, Liu Bei’s being a fierce hero seems to be a case of mistaking the appearance for the reality. As for Sun Quan alone, he has not yet been so labeled.
I have supplemented his statement with the following: The heroic and valiant Cao Mengde once also said, "When a son is born, he should be like Sun Zhongmou;
those such as the sons of Liu Jingsheng are nothing but piglets and dogs. Thus, Sun Quan’s heroism was truly that of a "heroic and valiant" one.
In this passage, the analogy of Cao [Mengde] clarifies the principle that all sentient beings are themselves Buddhas. It must...

Only when the garment of the five aggregates is removed does the mark of the Buddha’s manifestation appear; the analogy of Sun and Liu refers to the latter three [stages], hence it is said that the matter can be known through comparison, appearing clearly before one's eyes. △ Second, the analogy of the waves and moisture.
Furthermore, it is like when all waves are water and all water is waves: the characteristics of the waves are easily recognized, while the nature of wetness is difficult to manifest.
"All waves are water" is a metaphor for the entirety of the phenomena of the ten realms being contained within the principle of the three thousandfold world;

"all water is waves" is a metaphor for the entirety of the principle of the three thousandfold world arising as the phenomena of the ten realms. "The characteristics of the waves are easily recognized" is a metaphor for [the phenomena of] a single realm.
The manifestation of phenomena is as clear as if they were before one's eyes, yet their moist nature is difficult to manifest;

this is like the nature of the three thousand [realms] which lies hidden and is difficult to understand, becoming visible only upon removing one's clothes. △ Second, clarifying the subtlety and wonder of the Three Truths and Three Contemplations, part one:
clarifying the perfect fusion of the Three Truths. Sixth, first clarifying the origin of the Three Truths.

In this manner, the principle of reality possesses three distinct functions: the single principle of reality is the nature of emptiness as the *prativedha-hetu* (penetrating cause), the nature of the provisional as the *upāya-hetu* (expedient cause), and the nature of the mean as the *hetu-hetu* (causal cause).
The nature-endowed three thousand [dharmas] and the three causes explained in the preceding chapter constitute the essential substance of the three truths and the three contemplations.

In this present text, the intent is to clarify the phenomenal characteristics of the three truths and the three contemplations; thus, it further elucidates the reasons for establishing the truths and the contemplations.
This is solely because deluded attachments must be shattered; therefore, the methods of "immediately empty," "immediately provisional," and "immediately middle" are employed.
This is because it precisely clarifies the subtle and wondrous nature of the contemplation of the Truths, and further elucidates the origin of the Three Truths;
thus it says, "In this manner, the principle of the three thousand [realms] is perfectly present, and the three functions are fully manifest" (and so forth).

This is what is meant by our school’s teaching that "the cultivation arises entirely from the nature, and the cultivation is entirely within the nature. △ Second, explaining the reason for their mutual identity.
If the three truths were not inherently possessed (*xingju*), by what means could their meaning be established? It is not merely that the three thousand [dharmas] are the three truths;
rather, the three truths themselves are the three thousand.
The reason our school establishes that the true, the conventional, and the middle are mutually identical is precisely because they are all inherently possessed.

Therefore, if it were not for the inherent presence [of all phenomena] within nature (*prakṛti*), the principle of "immediacy" (*ji*) would not be established. Furthermore, regarding this principle of immediacy, there are two theories:
the horizontal (*tiryak*) and the vertical (*ūrdhva*). What was just stated concerning the mutual immediacy of the three truths (*triratna*) refers to the horizontal perspective.

As for the vertical perspective, it is not merely that the three thousand [phenomena] are immediate with the three truths; rather, it means that the reality of the entire three thousand is immediate with the principle of the three truths.
"Furthermore, the three truths are precisely the three thousand [realms]; this statement means that the principle of the three truths is entirely the phenomena of the three thousand.
This is because they are all of one essence and fundamentally non-dual. △ Third, the proof of the mutual identity of principle and phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that the Middle Truth (zhongdi) subsumes all phenomena, the Ultimate Truth (zhen di) dissolves all phenomena, and the Conventional Truth (su di) establishes all phenomena.
This is recorded in the Master Jingxi’s *Essentials of Mind from Beginning to End* (*Shizhong xinyao*), which states in brief: "As for the Three Truths, they are natural (*tianran*)."
This is the nature-virtue [of the Middle Way]. The Middle Truth (madhyama-satya) unifies all phenomena; the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya) dissolves all phenomena;
and the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya) establishes all phenomena. Master Yongjia’s commentary on the meaning states: "Middle" means not being biased toward either of the two extremes.
"Truth" (satya) means to examine and find it to be without falsehood. "Unify" means to encompass. "All phenomena" refers to the two extremes...
"True Dharma" means being without falsehood. "Extinction" (*miṇ*) means total dissolution. "All dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the three thousand realms.
"Worldly" refers to the mundane world. "Establishment" means to institute. "All dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the hundred worlds.

One should know that this explains the three truths according to their distinct aspects; if explained from the perspective of their universal integration, it should be said that they are one within the one.
In all things there is neither the Real (zhen) nor the Conventional (su); yet without being "middle" (zhong), the Three Truths are universally encompassed and free from dependence.
When one is real, all are real; without the middle and the conventional, if it were not real, the Three Truths would all vanish into extinction and be without characteristics.
When one is conventional, all are conventional; without the middle and the real, if it were not conventional, the Three Truths... [would likewise vanish].
All are established and remain distinct; by thoroughly studying this commentary, one will grasp the principle that the three thousand phenomena and the three truths are mutually identical.
△ Fourth, clarifying how they serve as guest and host: (1) First, the initial truth serves as the host.
The "three thousand" are identical with the Middle; taking the Middle as primary, they are one yet named three, which constitutes the fundamental objective realm of contemplation.
Since emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle are all attributes of the Middle, the Middle—which is identical to emptiness and provisional existence—returns to the two modes of cultivation.
In the following sections, the Three Truths all take the three thousand [dharmas] as their phenomenal realm (*śakyārtha*) and the Three Truths themselves as their noumenal realm (*tattvārtha*).

While the phenomena do not shift, their meanings are subsumed; thus, whether discussed through the Middle, the Empty, or the Provisional, the proponent and the opponent find that the reality of phenomena and principle remains exactly as it is, without addition or subtraction. Since this treatise takes the Middle as its primary focus, it addresses the three...
If one speaks from the perspective of the Middle as the central [teaching], then Emptiness and Provisionality are the attendants while the Middle is the host.
This is called "identity" (*ekatva*), yet in reality, "one" is not fixed as one; rather, the one necessarily possesses the three.

Within the Middle nature, the primary cause is the nature of emptiness, the completing cause is the nature of provisionality, and the auxiliary cause is the nature of the Middle. When these three causes are fully present, it is called "inherently existing."
When one contemplates the wondrous realm through the guests of emptiness and provisionality, the guest of the Middle comes to return to the host;
since both emptiness and provisionality then belong to the host, they are all categorized as "nature. However, if the Middle is not fixed as the Middle, then the host is not fixed as the host.

Therefore, the Middle is identical to emptiness and provisionality. When the host follows the guests, it returns to emptiness and provisionality; thus, the two practices of conditions and understanding are entirely cultivated within [the Middle].
This is what is meant by "the nature being complete and the nature giving rise to cultivation. One must understand that this refers to cultivation as inherently present within the nature itself;
it does not mean that one has already entered into the emptiness and conventionality of cultivated practice. △ Second, the True Truth (Paramārtha-satya) is primary.

The three thousand realms are themselves emptiness; with emptiness as the primary principle, this is called "the arising of cultivation from the entirety of nature. This constitutes the wondrous contemplation within the causal stage.
Since the provisional and the middle are both empty, all three belong to contemplation. Emptiness itself is the provisional and the middle, returning to the realm of function.

This clarifies that the objective realm of the three thousand phenomena is itself the objective realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). When explained, emptiness is the host and the provisional-middle (*prajñapti-madhyamaka*) is the guest;

while cultivation and manifestation are present, the fundamental nature and its function remain latent. Therefore, arising entirely from nature into cultivation is termed "the wondrous contemplation capable of observation within the cause.
Since both the provisional and the middle are empty, the guests return to the host; thus, all three belong to contemplation.
Emptiness is not fixed as emptiness, yet emptiness is itself the Middle and the Provisional; the host is not fixed as host, yet the host relates to the guest.
Thus, one returns to the realm of function. △ Third, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is taken as the host.
The three thousand realms are provisional, with the provisional as the primary principle; this is called the great function of liberation on the level of the fruit.
The empty and the middle are also provisional, and all three belong to the function. Thus, the provisional is identical to the empty and the middle, returning to the realm and the contemplation.

This explains the three thousand phenomena as the objective realm of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). When clarified, the conventional is taken as the host and the "emptiness within" (*śūnyatā*) as the guest;

thus, while the manifested objective realm is primary, the hidden aspect is secondary. Therefore, the "wondrous existence" (*myō-u*) is manifested as the great function of liberation on the level of the fruit.
Since both emptiness and the conventional are guests returning to the host, all three belong to the functional side, with the conventional being the foremost.
The mundane is not fixed, yet the mundane is itself empty; the host is not fixed, yet the host accords with the guest.
Thus, one returns to the contemplation of the objective realm. △ Fifth: Clarifying the Sublime Transcendence by Way of Contrast.
These three factors—each corresponding to two aspects—are discussed in the treatise as the three objects, the three contemplations, and the three functions.
They are neither identical nor separate, neither vertical nor horizontal; they are simultaneously both negation and illumination. This profound and wondrous principle is subtle and deep.
"Each corresponds to two clarities" means that they are explained in relation to the host and the guest.

For example, when the three thousand realms are identical with the Middle, the Middle serves as the host while emptiness and provisionality serve as the guests; these come to take refuge in the host of the Middle Truth. Thus, although there is one reality, it is given three names.
This is the wondrous object of contemplation which inherently exists. Since emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle all share the same nature, this constitutes a single object. This...
Regarding the clarification of the one: "The Middle is itself Emptiness; the Provisional is the host, and returning to it, one reverts to Emptiness and the Provisional.
Although these are called the two cultivations, they are actually cultivation within the nature; these are the three objects of contemplation. This is the clarification regarding the two.
Furthermore, as the Three Thousand Worlds are themselves Emptiness, Emptiness is the host and the Middle and Provisional are the guests, which then return [to Emptiness].
The Lord of True Reality is named "the Arising of Cultivation from the Total Nature"; this is the wondrous contemplation within the cause.

Because the provisional (*prajñapti*), the middle (*madhyama*), and the empty (*śūnya*)—all three—belong to contemplation, this constitutes a single contemplation; this is what is clarified by the phrase "one [contemplation] against one.

However, since emptiness is identical to the middle and the provisional, the subject returns to the guest, which is the middle and the provisional. Although these are called the object and its function, they constitute [the single contemplation].
The second of the two [aspects] within cultivation constitutes the three contemplations; this is explained in contrast to the two [preceding aspects].

Furthermore, the "three thousand" are identical to the provisional (*prajñapti*), with the provisional as the host and the empty and middle as guests; these return to the host of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and are termed the "great function of liberation on the level of fruition.
Since the empty, the middle, and the provisional all belong to function, they constitute a single function. This is it.
To clarify this through the first correspondence: although they are provisionally identical, emptiness is the host and the middle is the guest;

returning to the object and the contemplation constitutes these three functions. This clarifies it through the second correspondence. Because each of the three acts as host, object, and contemplation, they do not constitute a single identity;
because they must necessarily possess all three, they are not separate; and because they coexist within a single nature, they are not sequential. Thus, they are cultivated simultaneously.
Because the two natures are one, they are not horizontally established as separate; because they are empty, they are the middle; because they are the middle, they are the provisional;
and because they are the provisional, they are the illuminating. Since all three are fundamentally based on a single nature, these two meanings are simultaneous.

Tracing their source back to its origin, they are rooted in the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā); thus they are called "Mysterious" (xuan). Being spontaneously perfected from the beginning, they lack the coarseness of the three delusions; thus they are praised.
Because it is wondrous, profoundly deep, and bottomless, it is praised as "profound"; because it is free from all dependencies and oppositions, it is extolled as "absolute.
△ Sixth, the conclusion establishing Mahāparinirvāṇa:
Just as the three dots of the syllable *ī* are neither mixed with one another nor separated from one another, it is named Mahāparinirvāṇa.
This Dharma analogy originally derives from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The Sūtra says: "The secret treasury is like the three dots of the character *ī*;
if they are aligned horizontally, they do not form *ī*, and if they are aligned vertically, they also do not form *ī*.
Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara do they form *ī*. I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not yet *nirvāṇa*."
The body of the Tathāgata is not *nirvāṇa*, and the *mahāprajñā* is also not *nirvāṇa*; yet these three dharmas being distinct is likewise not *nirvāṇa*.
Now, I shall explain its meaning: "the secret treasury" refers to what is titled in the scripture as *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, which is translated here as "Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Great" (*mahā*) refers to the *dharmakāya*, and "extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*) refers to *prajñā*.
"Deliverance" (*tuo*) is liberation (*vimukti*); these three virtues are called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*).
Their arising in Buddhas and others is difficult to comprehend, and thus it is termed "secret" (*mi*). To say that one is three and three is one is termed "mysterious" (*mi*).
Containing all virtues within it, appearing as non-existent yet actually existing, is termed a "treasury" (*zang*). The phrase "like the letter *i*" is a metaphor. (End of Western [Commentary])
In the celestial Brahmī script, there is the letter *i*, which resembles the cursive style of this region:
the single dot above [·] is not like the vertical stroke of water [|]; the two dots below [· ·] are not like the horizontal strokes of fire [— —].
This is because the single dot above symbolizes the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; though it is but a single dot, it does not stand alone, for it possesses that which is below.

Because the two dots are positioned below, it is said: "Even if placed vertically, it does not form the character *ī*. The two dots below are a metaphor for the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and *vimukti* (liberation).
Although there are two dots below, because there is the single dot above them, they are not like the horizontal strokes of a blazing fire.
Therefore, it is said: "Even if placed side-by-side, it does not form the character *ī*; it must be like Maheśvara [the three-eyed deity]."
The three eyes on the face of Maheśvara form the character *i* (𑖀). This is a further explanation of the metaphor by means of another metaphor.

That all cultivation resides within the nature means that within cultivation, the nature is fully present;

That Tiantai took this as the wondrous seal for transmitting the mind was surely not without reason.

Nature is not something that can be severed or made non-existent; it merely reveals that these three thousand [realms] share a single identical characteristic.

Thus, because each and every one of the three thousand is itself nature, they are able to coexist within a single thought-moment. Furthermore, since a single thought-moment is itself emptiness, and since all things are identical to the one, how could they not be identical?

It is like the many jewels of Indra’s net: when one jewel is taken as the object of perception, the light of all the other jewels converges upon that single jewel.

Second is the contemplation of the provisional (*jia*).

Because they are identical with the provisional, all phenomena mutually include and encompass one another; their various characteristics are clearly manifest, and these three thousand realms do not lose their own essence.
One is all, yet even while they coexist within a single thought-moment, they are infinitely differentiated—just as when the reflection of a single pearl enters [a vessel].
The inconceivable multitude of jewels does not depend on provisional conditions;
rather, it takes the single thought-moment of consciousness as the object of contemplation.

By contemplating that the nature of this single thought-moment is replete with all phenomena (*dharmas*), and that these phenomena mutually contain and encompass one another, one realizes that there are not merely the ten realms and the hundred suchnesses, but indeed the hundred realms and the thousand [suchnesses].
Thus, there are not only ten realms with three hundred suchnesses, but also a thousand realms with ten thousand suchnesses;
there are not only a hundred realms with three thousand suchnesses, but also a thousand realms with thirty thousand suchnesses. When expanded and extended horizontally, they cannot be enumerated.

Since each and every one is mutually inclusive, each and every one is also mutually encompassing. Yet, because they are encompassed through mutual inclusion, they do not become a chaotic, disordered mass.
Moreover, each and every mark and realm is distinct and clearly manifest, such that their true nature (*tathatā*) is never obscured.

This is because the practitioner of provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-darśana*) is able to establish all phenomena and reveal these three thousand realms without losing their intrinsic essence; from the very first thought-moment, phenomena are such that one is all.
Therefore, although they coexist within a single thought-moment, the more one penetrates them, the more they are distinguished—just like a single pearl.
The light and shadows [of the sun] enter into the midst of the many jewels; such a wondrous Dharma is clearly understood by the Buddha alone and is not seen by others.

Furthermore, one may temporarily take a single thought-moment of consciousness as the object of contemplation.

By contemplating the nature of this single thought-moment as the Middle Way, one reveals that this nature is replete with the three thousand realms. It is not a single thought-moment, yet it is not the three thousand; because it is not a single thought-moment, it is not "one";
