Because it is central, when employing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one is not only able to shatter emotional attachments, but can also establish the Dharma and unify all phenomena.
To speak of the Dharma as "one emptiness, all emptiness," the three contemplations are all empty. Regarding the general contemplation of emptiness:

when using the contemplation of emptiness to contemplate the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*), the afflictions of view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the obstructing emotions are shattered; when contemplating the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the afflictions of the sands of dust [ignorance] are shattered.

When the obstructing emotions are broken through, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is revealed; when ignorance (avidyā) and the defiled obstructing emotions are broken through, the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) are overcome and the principle of the ultimate truth is revealed;

when the [afflictions] as numerous as motes of dust are broken through, the principle of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is revealed; and when ignorance is broken through, the principle of the middle way (madhyamā-pratipad) is revealed.
This is "one emptiness, all emptiness," which is collectively termed the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā). "One falsity, all falsity" refers to the three contemplations.

Regarding "all are provisional" and "the general provisional contemplation": when one uses provisional contemplation to contemplate the principle of the True Truth (*satyadharma*), the afflictions of view-delusion and thought-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and their obstructing emotions are seen to be empty;

when provisional contemplation contemplates the principle of the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the afflictions of the sands of phenomena (*rajas*) and their obstructing emotions are destroyed;

and when provisional contemplation establishes the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), the afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and their obstructing emotions are destroyed. This is called "one provisional [contemplation] encompassing all provisional [contemplations]" in a general sense.
This is the contemplation of the provisional (假觀). Within one, all are "middle" (中); thus, all three contemplations are the middle. Regarding the comprehensive contemplation of the middle (總中觀):
when the Middle Contemplation governs the Truth of Reality (真諦), it is not only the Middle Truth that can govern and be called the King of Dharmas; the Truth of Reality likewise is called the King.

When the defiled passions of view-delusion and thought-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) are empty, this negates existence; when the principle of the Truth of Reality is empty, this negates emptiness.
When the principle of True Reality (*tattva*) is revealed, it illuminates the emptiness of the three thousand worlds; when clarity is pure, it illuminates the conventional.

When observing the conventional truth through the Middle Way, the dust-like defilements of emotional attachments are shattered—this is the negation of the three thousand worlds of the conventional. When the principle is revealed, this is the negation of emptiness, which is precisely the negation of the conventional.

At the very moment of negating the conventional, one simultaneously illuminates emptiness; at the very moment of negating emptiness, one simultaneously illuminates existence. This is by means of the Middle Way.
Regarding the Middle Truth within contemplation, it simultaneously negates and illuminates both aspects with sovereign mastery; this goes without saying.

This is called "the Middle of One is the Middle of All," wherein all three contemplations are the Middle—this is the General Contemplation of the Middle. △ Third, clarifying the three contemplations by means of the simultaneous identity of negation and establishment.

This means that throughout the entire day one deconstructs characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and yet all dharmas are established; throughout the entire day one establishes dharmas and yet not even a speck of dust remains. Throughout the entire day one transcends all dependencies, while the two extremes (*antadvaya*) blaze forth.

This is to establish precisely as one deconstructs, and to deconstruct precisely as one establishes. It is neither deconstruction nor establishment, yet through non-deconstruction and non-establishment, there is deconstruction and establishment.

It is also called to illuminate precisely as one obstructs, and to obstruct precisely as one illuminates. It is neither obstruction nor illumination, yet through non-obstruction and non-illumination, there is obstruction.
As for the teaching on illumination, although the three contemplations proceed sequentially, they are practiced simultaneously.

When one is empty, all are empty; there is neither the provisional nor the middle that is not empty. All three contemplations are empty, constituting the universal contemplation of emptiness (*sāmānyatā-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Thus, while constantly deconstructing characteristics, all phenomena become purely provisional; when all are provisional, there is neither emptiness nor the middle.

The Middle does not rely on the three [other] contemplations; all are provisional, and the contemplation of the universal provisional is such that, although it establishes dharmas throughout the day, not even a speck of dust remains.
Within the One, all are the Middle; there is neither emptiness nor the provisional that is not the Middle.

This is the contemplation of the universal Middle, whereby one cuts off all dependencies throughout the day while the two extremes blaze forth. Therefore, it is said that at the very moment of negation, there is affirmation.
It is established at the very moment it is destroyed; it is not that there is destruction apart from the moment of establishment.
This refers to the function of the threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) in its establishment and destruction; explained through their perfect interfusion, it is thus:

one may substitute "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) for "destruction" and "illumination" (*āloka*) for "establishment," and likewise name this "simultaneous negation and illumination" and "simultaneous illumination and negation"—it is neither negation nor illumination.

Negation and illumination are expressed through provisional discourse, yet they possess a sequential order; however, upon reaching the perfect cultivation where emptiness and existence are simultaneous, negation and illumination occur within a single thought-moment, and in reality, no such sequence exists.
For the contemplation of causes establishes the truths, and those truths are manifested through contemplation;
therefore, without the threefold truth of perfect fusion, the threefold contemplation of perfect fusion cannot be accomplished. This is the ultimate of the Perfect and Sudden.
The nature of the Dharma is such that when other schools hear of it, many do not believe it, because it was originally established by Tiantai.
They do not realize that this principle is inherited distantly from Śākyamuni and directly received from Nāgārjuna;

that the three types of wisdom are truly attained within a single mind, and that through a single contemplation there are three contemplations, and by contemplating a single truth there are three truths.
"All phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare to be empty; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
This statement is still somewhat broad in its scope and may be difficult to accept with full conviction.

Only the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-śikhara-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Buddha’s Crown) proclaims this directly from the Buddha’s own lips, his holy words flowing forth in detail as he said: "I, by means of my wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—unify it with Suchness..."
Coming from the *ālayavijñāna*, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the wondrous, awakened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm;

even so, the *tathāgatagarbha*—the wondrously luminous, original mind—is not form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental objects, nor is it the three titles of the Tathāgata, nor permanence, bliss, self, or purity.
This is precisely the one reality where all is real; there is neither the conventional nor the middle, yet nothing is not real. It is the totality.

The True Truth (*satyadharma*) and the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is further said that the *tathāgatagarbha*—the primordial luminosity and wondrous mind—is identical to mind, identical to emptiness, and identical to form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects, even extending to the three titles and four virtues of the Tathāgata.

This is precisely the "all-false" (where everything is false), being neither true nor middle, yet not non-false; it is the Universal Falsehood (*panshi-di*) and the contemplation of the false (*jia-guan*).
It is further said: "The Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, is neither identical nor different, and is both identical and non-identical.

This precisely refers to the "all-encompassing within the one-encompassing," where there is neither the true nor the conventional, yet all is encompassed within the Middle Truth and the Middle Contemplation.
Thus we know that what was established by Tiantai deeply accords with the Buddha’s own mind; it is by means of this that he transmitted the seal of the Buddha-mind.
This is truly what is meant by "surpassing all doctrines and refuting the hundred schools. △ Fourth, establishing the correct and rejecting the erroneous to clarify the three contemplations:

If this were so, there would be no principle that could not be established and no insentient things that could not be sublated; how then would this differ from the emptiness of nihilistic annihilation or the provisional nature dependent on conditions?
Is this not to speak of departing from the two extremes and abiding in the Middle?

As for "no principle can stand without it," all three contemplations are capable of establishing principles; as for "no insentient thing is not destroyed by it," all three contemplations are capable of destroying delusions.
The Contemplation of Emptiness destroys the three delusions, whereby the Three Thousand Worlds and the Three Truths are revealed—not a mere annihilation into nothingness.
Through the contemplation of emptiness and the provisional, the three truths are established and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the hundred realms is revealed;

this does not depend on the provisional and the middle contemplations of dependent origination, through which the wondrous realm of the *dharmatā* appears by simultaneously negating and illuminating both extremes.
Furthermore, one should know that the fundamental principle of the Dharma-gates lies in the establishment of phenomena rather than their refutation; for while there are those who refute phenomena...
All these are done out of necessity. Establishing the Dharma is like employing civil governance (wen), while breaking the Dharma is like employing military force (wu).
Just as when a benevolent king reigns over the world his intent lies in civil governance, yet when the state is in chaos and the people are estranged, he must first employ military force;
so too do the three contemplations possess the merit of both breaking and establishing. Once the three delusions are broken, the principle of the three thousand realms is revealed.
Thus, the body becomes the wondrous form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the land becomes the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*);
only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively master all dharmas, and only then is their task fully accomplished. △ Third, it is explained that only Buddhas and Buddhas can know this.

Therefore it is said: "Only Buddha after Buddha can fully exhaustively realize this; even the two vehicles of rice-and-pea [śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas] and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot know even a small fraction of this meaning.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Stop, Śāriputra! There is no need to speak further. Why is this? Because of what the Buddha has accomplished."
Regarding this first, most rare and difficult-to-understand Dharma, which only a Buddha together with a Buddha can exhaustively fathom— the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena,
namely that all phenomena have such-and-such characteristics, such-and-such nature, and so forth, up to "such-and-such beginning, middle, and end, ultimately equal"—
one should know that the true reality of all phenomena exhaustively fathomed by all Buddhas is precisely what our own school [the Tiantai] has taken as its basis.

The three contemplations of the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) are the objects of contemplation—the ten realms and the three truths—which, when fully exhausted, constitute precisely what our school transmits as the mind-seal.
The single mind that is able to contemplate these is the three contemplations. These three contemplations, when present in the causal stage, are collectively termed the "Single Mind";
when they reach the perfect penetration of the six sense faculties, they are termed the "Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision" at the stage of fruition. However—
There are four distinct stages—opening, showing, awakening, and entering. If one wishes to exhaustively investigate these to their ultimate limit, it lies solely with the Buddhas;

therefore, it is said, "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively investigate them," and also, "Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust all their thought to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Even if the ten directions were filled with [beings like him]..."
Śāriputra and the other disciples likewise filled the lands of the ten directions; though they exhausted their thoughts to measure it together, they still could not know it.

This is because the wisdom of the śrāvakas—even that of Śāriputra—is but a one-sided wisdom of emptiness, which regards the extinction of the body and the cessation of cognition as the ultimate goal, and perceives only the single emptiness within the threefold contemplation of the one mind.
Because all things are empty and there is no mutual interaction between them, one cannot know even a small portion [of the Buddha's wisdom]. Furthermore, it is said that even Pratyekabuddhas—
those of sharp intelligence, free from outflows, in their final body, and as numerous as the bamboos filling the ten directions—
even if they were to focus their minds together for immeasurable billions of kalpas, would be unable to know even a small portion of the Buddha’s true wisdom.

This is because, although the wisdom of partial emptiness excels that of the Śrāvakas by severing both afflictions and habitual tendencies, it has no connection whatsoever with the "one mind and three contemplations" wherein "one is empty and all are empty. Thus it is said: "The two vehicles, like rice and hemp, do not know this meaning.
Furthermore, it is said: "Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, having made offerings to countless Buddhas, have thoroughly realized..."
Furthermore, regarding the various meanings and purposes, they are also able to skillfully expound the Dharma, filling the worlds of the ten directions like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.
Even if those with a single mind and wondrous wisdom were to contemplate them together throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they could not know the Buddha’s wisdom.

This statement refers to bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, who—by means of the wisdom that issues from the provisional—comprehend the meanings and purposes and skillfully expound the Dharma.
Although they surpass the two vehicles, because they cannot yet fully comprehend the wisdom of the three contemplations— in which "the one is entirely provisional"—
they are unable to know the Buddha-wisdom in which the provisional and the real are mutually identical within the single mind of the three contemplations. Furthermore,

it is said that even if bodhisattvas at the stage of non-retrogression were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and sought to contemplate this together with a single mind, they still could not know it.
This means that although Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching cultivate the wisdom of "only-middle" and thus attain the three grades of non-retrogression,
they are unable to comprehend the principle of the perfect fusion of the three contemplations— wherein taking one is to take all three, and speaking of the three is to speak of each as one—
and wherein within every single middle there is neither the real nor the provisional. Therefore, even if they contemplate and seek together with a single mind, [they cannot realize it].

Furthermore, they are unable to know; all of this is spoken in terms of whether one knows or does not know based on the superiority or inferiority of the mind, and is not initially discussed in terms of the high or low status of one's rank.
For example, when the imperial court establishes offices and assigns duties, ordinary scholars merely follow in the dust of others' footsteps;
yet when it comes to winning victory at the examination halls, even those of long-standing official service must yield to their juniors. This is why...
That the Buddha praised the initial resolve of one of Perfect Capacity as being like the kalaviṅka chick whose cry surpasses that of all other birds,

and that the Crown Prince’s nobility while in the womb eclipsed all his ministers— these serve to further awaken one to this principle. △ Fourth, it is clarified that this purport resides precisely in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Thus, while the three thousand realms throughout all sections in the *Lotus Sūtra* (the *Dharmaparyāya of the White Lotus of the True Dharma*) involve both the fault of overlapping inclusion and the error of separation and partiality,
the present sūtra is not only pure and free from admixture, but is further able to reveal the coarse as the sublime.
That the title calls it the "Sublime Dharma" (*Saddharma*) is precisely because of this.
Regarding the general reliance upon various schools, as previously stated, different names are established within the various Mahāyāna traditions:

first, according to the *Avataṃsaka*, [the Buddha-nature] is divided into the ten directions according to the conditions of defilement and purity; second, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
third, according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, both icchantikas and virtuous persons possess both the nature of goodness and the nature of evil as causes.
First, the *Sutra on the Universal Gateway of Avalokiteśvara* relies solely on [the aspect of] "invocation," while the [sutra on] "Poisonous Harm" relies on both;

nevertheless, if one considers the primary intent, it lies precisely in the *Lotus Sūtra*. This is because although the teachings of the former sutras are indeed wondrous, they nonetheless fall into two partialities, thereby incurring the fault of being merely "inclusive" (i.e., partial) and the error of "separating" the partial. This is precisely because the *Avataṃsaka* is not only...

There is the fault of conflating the three contemplations of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) with those of the Perfect-Sudden Teaching (*paripūrṇa-akṣaya-darśana*), thereby committing the error of making the Perfect-Sudden forever separated from the Separate.
In the Vaipulya sūtras, the perfect contemplation is elucidated by contrasting it with the partial contemplation;

in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, the perfect contemplation is elucidated while incorporating the partial contemplation. In these two periods as well, there is nothing that does not [function in this manner].
The distinction between the Perfect and the Partial is fully present in various sutras such as the Vimalakīrti; I shall not cite them here at length.
This present sutra intends to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

It brings the three vehicles together into the One Buddha Vehicle, and all nine realms return to the one Buddha-realm. Thus, it avoids the fault of prior partiality while being able to open up the previous three vehicles.
The coarse aspects of the nine realms are integrated with the subtle and profound wonder of the One Vehicle;

it is like the ninefold elixir of the immortals, which not only enables one who ingests it to return to the source and restore the fundamental, but also enables one to cast off the bones and ascend as an immortal.
Therefore, the title of the sutra calls it the "Sublime Dharma" (Miaofa), for it possesses these two wonders: first, the wonder of mutual dependence (*xiangdai miao*). That is to say—

There is no longer any coarseness of prior "combined" or "concurrent" [teachings]; rather, the two types of "absolute" (dualistic) subtlety open up all those previous coarse elements so that they all become subtle.
This is as the Venerable Śāriputra’s realization stated: "Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha;
born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, I have obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma. To say one has "obtained a portion" means that by means of oneself...
Realizing the wisdom of partial emptiness, one is able to understand that when all is empty, there is neither the provisional nor the middle that is not empty;
yet, although there is nothing that is not empty, this is precisely the emptiness of differentiation. Therefore, it is said that one "attains a portion of the Buddha-dharma.
This refers to the marvelous principle of taking the relative as the absolute. Mahākāśyapa and the other four great elders also spoke thus.
Now, the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously; all that a son of the Buddha ought to await has already been obtained.
This realization is absolute, yet it serves as the subtle excellence of the relative. △ Fifth, the manifestation of the subtle excellence of contemplation through analogy.
Thus we know that taking this absolute, wondrous Dharma as the essence of contemplation is comparable to sunlight not coexisting with darkness.

As clarified previously, taking the absolute, wondrous Dharma as the essence of contemplation means that the principle-essence of the three contemplations universally relies upon all sections [of the teachings];

specifically, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it resides in the three thousand dharmas, the three truths, the nature of good and evil, the three causes, and the three virtues—all of which are absolute.
Regarding the essence of this contemplation: why is this so? Because other schools, though they know that nature is replete with good, do not know that nature is replete with evil.

Therefore, one must necessarily rely upon the cultivated evil of the nine realms to manifest the cultivated good of the Buddha-realm, thereby contemplating the three truths and accomplishing the three contemplations.
Whether one practices emptiness, the provisional, or the middle exclusively—such practice is termed [the "gradual"].

Taking the subtlety of mutual dependence as the essence of contemplation: when one contemplates the nine realms’ cultivated evil as having both direct and contributive conditions that are identical to inherent evil, and when inherent evil is interfused such that there is no dharma that does not spontaneously accord with it, thereby encompassing the Buddha-realm’s inherent goodness, this is the essence of the contemplation of absolute transcendence.
Because it can be compared to nothing else, it is said to be "like the light of the sun."

In the "Section on the Doctrinal Characteristics" (*kyōsō*) of the *Dharmapada-sūtra Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), the Great Master does not share this [interpretation] with those in the dark;
he elaborates upon the three similes from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to form five similes. The three similes from the *Avataṃsaka* are as follows: first, the sun rises and shines upon the high mountains;
second, it shines upon the deep valleys; and third, it shines upon the level plains. The Great Master elaborates upon the simile of the level plains to form three [further] commonalities.
It is like the five periods [of the sun's course], which are like the sun at its rising: first it illuminates the high mountains, which is like the *Avataṃsaka*;
next it illuminates the deep valleys, which is like the *Tripiṭaka*; next it illuminates the level plains, which is like the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Vaipulya*;

next it illuminates the forenoon, which is like the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*; as explained extensively therein; and finally, when the solar disk halts at midday, its light shines universally upon both the high and the low.

All are made equal and impartial; when the shadow cast by the soil-gauge is neither diminished nor increased, those who are like one with bowed head, or of low voice, or distracted, or of slight virtue, all attain the path of Buddhahood.
No one is allowed to attain extinction alone; rather, they are all brought to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
Because it is as described in this present sutra, it is said: "For example, just as the light of the sun does not [discriminate]..."
Darkly shared. △ Sixth, concluding with the discourse on the ultimate to form the Mind Seal (Cixin).
This is the final, ultimate, and most profound teaching; it constitutes the authentic transmission of the Mind Seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

To speak of the ultimate and final conclusion: the Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*), desiring to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*).

As for the phrase "desiring to cause sentient beings," this refers to sentient beings of the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*). If there were even a single realm that did not attain the Buddha-way, it would be said that [the purpose] was not fulfilled.
To fully realize the Tathāgata’s original intention: although the *Avataṃsaka* is said to "first illuminate the high mountains," it does not proceed from a gradual approach;
yet, while it enables Bodhisattvas to achieve the Buddha-way, it cannot enable those Śrāvakas in the assembly—who are like the deaf or the mute—to achieve the Buddha-way.
This is merely the initial teaching and a partial teaching; it is insufficient to serve as the ultimate consummation.
To exhaustively and ultimately explain how the true mind-seal transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs is contained within the twelve years of exclusively teaching the Small Vehicle—

this need not even be mentioned, as it is insufficient to correspond to it. Furthermore, although during the eight years of the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings he addressed the small with the great and the biased with the perfect,
the lands he manifested still had purity and defilement, and his physical manifestations varied in scale from vast to minute.
The power of teaching the Dharma according to understanding and the inconceivable powers are unique;

therefore, one perceives purity and impurity, hears praise and censure, smells the scent of *campaka* flowers and not the *atimuktaka*, experiences attachment to the body and non-attachment to the body, and possesses wisdom that is manifold or not manifold.
This, however, is merely a gradual teaching and a partial exposition; it is insufficient to correspond to the ultimate, final, and most profound teaching.

The direct transmission of the mind-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like the Prajñāpāramitā; although it contains both the general and specific expositions, it primarily teaches the Perfect Teaching.
However, it speaks only of actual phenomena for the sake of Bodhisattvas and does not speak of this true essence for my sake.

Furthermore, it is insufficient as the ultimate, final, and most profound teaching. Only the Dharma of the Ultimate Reality constitutes the direct transmission of the mind-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Since the flowers have already passed through the various methods of mediation by the Venerable Xiang, and their fundamental natures are now pure, they are worthy of receiving the Seal of the Mind.

The two kinds of wisdom—the provisional and the real—converge into a single essence. The ultimate reality of all phenomena within the ten realms is such that all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood.
All worldly appearances are nothing but eternal; the sprouts that withered in the past [shall likewise flourish].
Among those who have sown seeds that were ruined, there are none who do not sprout the shoots of the Way; for lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land.
One by one they receive the Buddha’s lotus-flower prediction: Śāriputra received his prediction from the Buddha Padmaprabha first, and from the Buddha Prabhāsa next after Kāśyapa.
Therefore it is said: "This is the ultimate, final, and most profound teaching. This is what it means.
This is the direct transmission of the mind-seal from the Buddhas and Patriarchs. △ Second, clarifying the traces of the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal, in two parts.

First, clarifying the traces of his own practice, in four parts. First, correctly clarifying the ancestral succession, in two parts. First, clarifying the ancestral succession as spoken by the Golden Mouth, in five parts.
First, the transmission to Kāśyapa.
The Buddha transmitted this to Kāśyapa.

There are both general and specific aspects to the Buddha’s transmission to Kāśyapa. The general aspect refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; the specific aspect refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Regarding the general aspect, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra during the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this [is taught by] all Buddhas..."
When the Tathāgata spoke these words, Śāriputra attained realization regarding this Dharma teaching.
The World-Honored One then conferred upon him the prediction that he would become a Buddha in the future, named Puṣpārāma. Furthermore, he addressed Śāriputra:
"I shall now employ a further parable to clarify this meaning. He then spoke of a great house where a fire suddenly broke out, and how the elder used skillful means.

The Tathāgata is also like this: first, he teaches the three vehicles to entice and guide sentient beings, leading them out [of saṃsāra], and subsequently bestows upon them all equally the high, wide, and great white ox-carts. At that time, Mahākāśyapa and the others—
The four great śrāvakas, having attained realization at this point, then spoke the parable of the impoverished son: "It was as if an impoverished son abandoned his father and fled;
more than fifty years later, although he encountered him again, his disposition remained base and inferior. For twenty years, he was constantly made to clear away dung.
After this period, their minds came to trust one another through mutual understanding, they were reunited as father and son, and he was truly established in the inheritance of the house."

The karmic agents themselves said: "From the past until now, we have delighted only in the Lesser Dharma. The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, has preached the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
only now do we realize that the World-Honored One is not at all stingy regarding the Buddha-wisdom.
Therefore, we say that originally we had no intention to seek anything, yet now this great treasure of the Dharma King has come to us spontaneously."
"Whatever a son of the Buddha ought to attain, you have already attained it all.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa, employing the parable of the medicinal herbs to further elucidate and confirm his understanding, saying to him:
"In the future, you shall become a Buddha named *Prabhāsa* (Light). Furthermore, regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it says: 'The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: I now...'"
All the unsurpassed True Dharma is hereby entrusted to Kāśyapa; he shall serve as your great reliance.
Thus, the transmission through which Kāśyapa attained realization was already established at the assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
However, because the conditions for those to be transformed by the Tathāgata were nearing their end while the conditions for Kāśyapa were about to flourish, it was separately entrusted to him.

This is to let the fourfold assembly know that the karmic conditions for realization reside within them. For the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the *Lotus Sūtra* is none other than the wondrous mind of the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, those who transmit the Buddha’s seal of the mind are not limited to a single individual;
on the occasion of the *Lotus Assembly*, everyone who received the prediction of enlightenment attained it. If one were to discuss the three grades of faculties, Śāriputra was foremost among them.

Since the Dharma realized by the predecessors is identical to that bestowed upon their successors, and the predictions they received do not differ, how could there be any disparity in the Dharma due to the sequence of their realizations? △ Second, the successive transmission through the generations.
Kāśyapa transmitted this to Ānanda. Within this [tradition], there are both general and specific aspects;
the general aspect is that they both participated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Buddha told Ānanda:
'In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Oceanic Wisdom.'"

As for the distinction between their coming and parting, it pertains to Kāśyapa; thus, the *Dharma-transmission Chronicle* states that when Kāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the most supreme Dharma to Ānanda and spoke as follows [and so forth]. This account refers to the general transmission of the Dharma;
nevertheless, it does not preclude Ānanda from regarding Kāśyapa as his elder brother, nor Kāśyapa from treating him as his younger brother.

Ānanda spoke thus in reference to the distinct succession of the transmission of the Dharma; yet this did not prevent Ānanda from serving Kāśyapa as his teacher, nor did it prevent Kāśyapa from treating Ānanda as his son.
This was precisely because the public concern lay in the transmission of the Dharma, such that formal hierarchical order need not be observed.
Ānanda entered the *vāyu-samādhi* (wind-samādhi) by the river and divided his body into four streams of Dharma.
The Dharma was entrusted to Śāṇakavāsin: the teaching on the manifestation of the five hundred Dharma-gates by raining down nectar from the palms of the hands. The Dharma was entrusted to Upagupta:
the teaching on attaining the third fruit while still a layperson and attaining the fourth fruit upon receiving the precepts. The Dharma was entrusted to Tiṣya:

the teaching on attaining the first fruit upon ascending the altar and attaining the fourth fruit through the three *karmavācanās*. The Dharma was entrusted to Mitraka. The Dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa. The Dharma was entrusted to the Buddha.
Dhānañjāni was entrusted with the Buddha’s secret teachings; he conferred the Three Refuges upon King Prasenajit and subdued the practitioners of calculation.
To the Bhikṣu Pārśva, who emerged from the womb with white hair and whose hands emitted light, the method for taking up the sūtras was entrusted.
To Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, the method for debating and excelling was entrusted; he caused Aśvaghoṣa to shave his head and become his disciple. Aśvaghoṣa composed the *Rāṣṭrapāla-kāvya*.

The courtesan Gītapriyā expounded impermanence, suffering, and emptiness; those who heard her awakened to the Dharma. She transmitted the Dharma to Kāpimāra, who composed the *Treatise on Non-Self* (*Anātma-śāstra*).
Wherever this treatise spread, false views were extinguished. He transmitted the Dharma to Nāgārjuna. Nāgārjuna was born with both a physical body and a Dharma-body;
he composed the *Treatise on the Great Compassion of Expedient Means* in five thousand stanzas and the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Great Ornament Treatise) in five [thousand stanzas].

The *Thousand Verses on Great Fearlessness* (*Sahasraślokābhayamahārāja-śāstra*), the *One Hundred Thousand Verses of the Upadeśa-śāstra*, the *One Hundred Thousand Verses of the Dharma-putra-kanadeva*,
the method for bestowing the divine eye upon ten thousand people with physical eyes, the method for bestowing [the teachings] upon Rāhula,
the book containing the names of many spirits, the method for subduing non-Buddhists, and the method for testing [disciples] by means of verses spoken by Saṃkhyanandita.
The Dharma was entrusted to Saṃghayaśas; while traveling by sea, he saw a city and spoke a verse on the Dharma. It was entrusted to Kumārajīva;
he saw ten thousand cavalry and, by noting the color of the horses, obtained the name [of the place]. He was entrusted with the method for distinguishing robes. It was entrusted to Śayananda;
for a person who had committed a grave offense, he prepared a fire pit and made him enter it to repent. When the pit became a pond, his sin was extinguished. It was entrusted to [the Dharma].

Vasubandhu bestowed the Dharma upon Mañjuśrī; he divided the Gaṅgā River into two parts and personally transformed one part [into a river] to bestow the Dharma upon Kṣemendra. △ Third, the transmission to Śiṃha.
The lineage was transmitted down through twenty-four generations until it reached the Bhikṣu Siṃha.
To Siṃha, Haklenayana entrusted the Dharma; however, Siṃha was killed by King Dāmila, who slew him with a sword from which milk flowed.
From Kāśyapa to Siṃha, there were twenty-three persons who held the *Dharmakośa*. [The last was] Madhyāntika.

If one were to take them up simultaneously with Śāṇakavāsin, there would be twenty-four people; all these masters were recorded by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] as being saints capable of bringing great benefit.
In the past, kings did not establish stables within monasteries, but established stables at slaughterhouses;
how much more so when encountering a Sage in a fortunate age—could it not be beneficial? Furthermore, regarding the Brahmin who sold the skull-bone of Koṇḍañña:

The merit of those who are half-way, those who are not [half-way], and those who have attained realization, in building stupas for offerings and thereby attaining birth in the heavens and hearing the essentials of the Dharma, is such as this.
For the sake of these benefits, the Buddha entrusted the Dharma-treasury (the *Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*). △ Fourth, pointing to the authorities relied upon.

The master Siṃha encountered difficulties and did not transmit [the teaching]; thus, these constitute the ancestral succession from the Golden Mouth (the Buddha), all of whom were those who attained realization through direct vision.
This is recorded in the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (付法傳).
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (付法藏因緣經) states: "Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Siṃha in the kingdom of Kaśmīra."
While he was performing great deeds of Buddha-work, there was a king named Mīrakhura whose wrong views were rampant and whose mind lacked true faith.
In the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he destroyed stūpas and monasteries and slaughtered the assembly of monks. He then used a sharp sword to sever the head of the Lion;
from within the head, no blood flowed, but only milk. Thus, the transmission of the Dharma masters was cut off.
This is because what the Great Master Xugxi taught was based on authentic sources and was not merely a fabrication;
those who "know it through seeing" are those who personally witnessed the transmission between master and disciple.

Furthermore, that which is understood from the sutras and treatises may be called "knowing through hearing," and that which is received through direct oral instruction and personal guidance may likewise be so named.
To know through hearing is like receiving a transmission from paper and ink; this may also be called "knowing through seeing.
The matter lies in how one applies it; there is no fixed location for it. △ Fifth, the addition of the chanting of other schools.

Some claim that the verses spoken by the six preceding Buddhas and the four patriarchs, the entrustment of the Dharma, the plucking of the flower, and the smile, constitute a "special transmission outside the teachings" (jiaowai biechuan);
however, as there is no scriptural authority for this, everyone rejects it.
I have annotated this far and have long since ceased my pen. Yet, some who were not satisfied with this explanation asked me from the side:
"Master Huxi composed the *Fozu xinian ji* (Record of the Mind-Seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) to propagate the Way of Tiantai;
that was sufficient. Why must you now pick at every hair and seek out flaws, recklessly creating right and wrong to such an extent? Master!"
"Since you have already composed a commentary on this, why not synthesize these two traditions to establish for future generations the Samādhi of Non-contention?

I replied, "Yes, yes; no, no. He asked again, "Why is that so? I said, "The 'Plucking the Flower' and the 'Smile' constitute the separate transmission outside the teachings, which does not rely on words and letters, but directly points to the human mind to see one's nature."
To achieve Buddhahood through this Zen school is the grand discourse on the Buddha-dharma and its profound purport;

it is precisely the wondrous principle of Tiantai’s contemplation of the mind as the true mark (dharmatā)—a state free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of written words, and free from the marks of mental objects.
How could there be any difference between them? Since it is further said that "directly pointing at the human mind, seeing one's nature, and attaining Buddhahood," what else remains?
Since the existence of words is already non-existent, and even more so when there are no words, what teaching could there possibly be?
This is precisely what Tiantai meant when he said that hearing the teaching naturally leads to contemplating the mind; only by departing from the finger can one recognize the moon.

Thus, it may rightly be called the "separate transmission outside the teachings" where "words and letters are not established. How much more so for the Chan school! However, as for Tiantai’s non-establishment of texts...
Furthermore, Master [Zongmi] has never maintained that the absence of speech constitutes existence or that the presence of speech constitutes non-existence, as Vimalakīrti said:

"One does not depart from words to speak of the characteristics of liberation. Thus, when this school uses this to discuss the teachings, it may be called the "Great Teaching" (Dajiao) and the "Orthodox Transmission" (Zhengzhuan);
when it uses this to discuss contemplation, it may also be called the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings" (Jiaowai Bietuan). Why should it be unique [to one category]?

Tiantai said that Bodhidharma stated, "I have the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* with which to seal the mind," and it is appropriate to designate this as the orthodox transmission of the Great Teaching.
For this reason, throughout the fifth and sixth generations of the Chan school, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was held in high esteem;
furthermore, during the Yongming era, [Yanshou] extensively cited the sincere words of the Buddhas and patriarchs to create the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) for the first time.
If one speaks thus, it is clear that the teaching cannot be discarded; likewise, it is also clear that Chan cannot be discarded.
While the Master of Huxi’s assertion is indeed too extreme, since there is no basis in the sutras or śāstras, it is difficult to even speak of his position, which everyone rejects.
Why is this? It is precisely because after the time of Śāriputra, the Chan school...

Supporting the *Dhyāna Sūtra*, he established twenty-eight patriarchal generations and further rejected the *Fu fa zuan* (Record of the Transmission of the Dharma), claiming that its conclusion with Siṃha was erroneous.

While such vigorous disputes were not limited to this day alone, at that time, Chan Master Song Mingjiao based himself on the *Dhyāna Sūtra* to produce the *Dingzu tu* (Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs), asserting that the *Fu fa zuan* should be consigned to the flames; meanwhile, Pu [Jingxiu] of Wuxing...

The Master Puzhao once composed the *Zushuo* (Discourse on the Patriarchs) to rescue [the tradition], yet three years later, when Master Yongshou realized that there were points in the *Chanjing* (Sutra of Meditation) that did not accord with reason, he remarked that these must have been errors in the transcription process. Master Puzhao again composed the *Zhice* (Refuting Errors) to refute him;
its general purport states: "Yongshou established twenty-eight patriarchs based falsely upon the *Chanjing*, thereby deluding the world. I [the author] condemn this.
The *Fofazang* (Treasury of the Dharma Transmission) is a spurious work.

This arose because the Tang dynasty’s Zhi Ju, in composing the *Baolin Zhuan*, saw that the *Chanjing* (Dhyāna Sūtra) listed nine persons, with the eighth named Dharmatrāta and the ninth named Prajñātāra.
Upon seeing the two characters "Da-mo" (Dharma), Zhi Ju moved him [Bodhidharma] to the position after Prajñātāra and further appropriated [the lineage].

Elsewhere, he lists two names—Vasudhara and Ratnamati—to supplement the twenty-four, totaling twenty-eight "torches," which he falsely presents at the beginning while Huiyuan’s errors are appended at the end;
thus he violates and confuses the orthodox teaching, bringing blemish upon the Chan school.
I once confronted him face-to-face regarding this, yet Huiyuan showed no shame. Furthermore, according to Sengyou’s *San*... [text truncated]
In the *Zangji*, the lineage of the Vinaya patriarchs is recorded as consisting of fifty-three persons, the last of whom is named Dharmatrāta;
yet Zhiju takes this to refer to the Dharmatrāta of the Liang dynasty. This is a profound ignorance of the fact that what Sengyou recorded refers to those who propagated the Hinayana Vinaya.
Since Huishou already revered the Zen patriarchs as Mahayana, how could he have conversely employed the Hinayana Vinaya?

If even the human patriarchs are thus, how much more so the case with the Chan scriptures? Furthermore, they lack the names of the twenty-eight patriarchs and clarify only the śrāvaka Hīnayāna dhyāna as recorded in the *Sanzang ji*.
Since Huikou lacked the eye of the teachings, upon seeing the mere word "Chan," he claimed it as his own school;
this was nothing less than a reversal of the legacy of Bodhidharma of the Liang dynasty, who transmitted only the methods of Hīnayāna dhyāna.
"To falsely accuse the former sages is no small transgression" (*Fozu tongji*). From this one may know that the sutras and śāstras lack authority and that everyone rejects them;
the fault lies with later generations and does not concern Bodhidharma.
Thus, the Dharma Master Zhipan of Siming once provided an explanation, saying: "The Buddha attained the recollection of past lives and the prediction of future accomplishment."
Although the Way may surely allow for foreknowledge across billions of kalpas, why is it that the records of the patriarchs now stop at only twenty-four?

I venture to infer the Buddha’s intention based on two principles: first, that the Lion [Bodhisattva] encountered a life-threatening peril as one of the singular hardships in the transmission and upholding of the Dharma;
second, that although there have been successors to the patriarchate since then, they likely do not compare to the Great Sages who were the Four Reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).
For this reason, the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] spoke thus, not intending to say that there was no succession of the patriarchs.
Some in the world claim that because Śiṃha encountered misfortune, the Dharma was not transmitted; such words are merely those of the foolish.

Our school maintains that the lineage of the patriarchs ended with Śiṃha, yet the Zen forests add four more individuals; thus, they compete in mutual censure for successive generations without ceasing. Let us test this with a broad perspective.

If one resolves this matter, there is nothing that constitutes an obstacle: although the Lion [the Buddha] encountered the perils of life, it was not that he had no disciples capable of transmitting the Dharma;
it was simply that they were not among those specifically recorded in the golden mouth’s prophecy.
Thus, adding four more individuals until we reach Dharmatrāta, who first brought [the teaching] to the Eastern Land, these are called the twenty-eight patriarchs.
It would have been sufficient to say that the Dharma was transmitted through four successive generations;
yet, to now falsely cite the *Candragarbha-sūtra* as proof is only to invite further unreliability for oneself.

When Sōng Míngjiào produced his "Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs," he claimed that the *Candragarbha-sūtra* fully records twenty-eight patriarchs; however, upon examining the sūtra, only nine individuals are listed.
It is appropriate that Master Puzhao Fang corrects these errors and refutes them, as their names are many and inconsistent. △ Second, clarifying the ancestral transmission of Tiantai.
Part one: Correctly clarifying the ancestral transmission. Section four: The Great Dharma’s transmission to the East.
By the time of Emperor Ming of the Han, the Buddha-dharma flowed to the East following a night dream.

The *Tongji* states: In the seventh year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man sixteen feet tall with a halo like sunlight upon his head, flying through the palace courtyard.
In the morning, he questioned his ministers, but none could provide an answer. The Grand Historian Fu Yi then stepped forward and said:
Your servant has heard that during the time of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, a sage appeared in the west whose name was Buddha.
Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched the General-in-Chief Qin Jing, the Court Scholar Wang Zun, and eighteen others as envoys to the Western Regions to seek the Way of the Buddha.
After ten years, Cai Yin and his companions encountered Kāśyapa in the kingdom of the Great Yuezhi in Central India.
Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna obtained a standing image of the Buddha and a Sanskrit manuscript of the scriptures consisting of six hundred thousand words;
they brought these on white horses to Luoyang. Mātanga and Ratna, appearing in the robes of śramaṇas, were received by the Emperor and lodged at the Court of State Ceremonial.

In the eleventh year [of the reign], an imperial decree was issued to establish the Baima Monastery (White Horse Monastery) outside the Yong Gate to the west of Luoyang. There, Mātanga first translated forty [scrolls].

In the second chapter, it is recorded that the Sanskrit texts of the Sūtra Piṭaka were kept in the stone chambers of the Imperial Library, and images of the Buddha were depicted at the Xiyang City Gate and atop Mount Xianjie.
This marks the beginning of the presence of the Three Jewels in this eastern land.

From the Western Han through the Eastern Han, and on into the Wei, Jin, and Six Dynasties periods, there was never a lack of individuals seeking the Dharma from India; those who translated [the scriptures] in this eastern land [were likewise numerous].
As for the *sūtras*, there were those possessing virtue in the world during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty;
Kumārajīva translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-śīla-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* under the Yao Qin.

These several translations all serve as the foundation for entering into awakening according to Tiantai. △ Second, the Horizontal School of the Northern Qi (3): First, explaining the origins of its doctrine.

During the Northern Qi period, there was Master Huiwen, who, upon investigating the *Śāstra on the Great Perfection of Wisdom*, awakened to the single mind and the threefold wisdom, thereby directly inheriting the tradition of Nāgārjuna.

Having long been endowed with the Perfect Vehicle and possessing innate, solitary awakening, he read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which cites the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* as follows:
One who wishes to fulfill the knowledge of the paths with the knowledge of the paths should study the Prajñāpāramitā;

one who wishes to fulfill all-knowledge with the knowledge of the paths should study the Prajñāpāramitā; one who wishes to fulfill the knowledge of all modes with all-knowledge should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
one who wishes to sever the afflictions along with their residual impressions with the knowledge of all modes should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

The treatise asks itself: "If one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as the abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*), within a single moment of mind, why is it now said that 'one fulfills knowledge of all aspects by means of all-knowledge,' and 'one abandons the afflictions and their residual impressions by means of knowledge of all aspects'? The answer is: "In reality, all are attained simultaneously."
In this context, in order to inspire faith in the Prajñāpāramitā, these distinctions are explained in sequence so that sentient beings may attain a pure mind;

therefore, it is taught in this way. Furthermore, although [these stages] are attained within a single moment of mind, there is still a sequence of beginning, middle, and end, just as within a single moment of mind there arise the causes and conditions for the arising, abiding, and the cause of abiding of the three characteristics.
The cessation of conditions is likewise like the mind and mental factors, the dissociated formations, and the bodily and vocal actions.
Through the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), one fulfills all-knowledge (*sarvajñāna*); through all-knowledge, one fulfills the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);

and through the knowledge of all modes, one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The Master, relying on this text, cultivated the contemplation of the mind accordingly.
In the *Treatise*, it is stated that the three wisdoms are actually attained within a single mind; since the fruit is attained in one mind, how could the causes be acquired sequentially?

Therefore, when this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the three wisdoms in a single mind—where both are simultaneously negated and simultaneously illuminated—and thus enters the stage of the first dwelling, the rank of the non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, while reading the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, the Master came across the verse in the Chapter on the Four Truths which says:
"Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I say they are empty; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
With sudden and clear awakening, one realizes that all phenomena are none other than those produced by causes and conditions.

These causes and conditions are not fixed as existent, nor are they fixed as empty; that emptiness and existence are non-dual is what is called the Middle Way. The Master has already [taught] this as one.
According to the *Śāstra*, it is known that he inherits the lineage distantly from Nāgārjuna (*Tǒngjì*). △ Second, clarifying the tracing of the source:
if one traces him upward, he is the thirteenth master among the twenty-four patriarchs.
△ Third, the transmission through hearing and knowing.
Master Wen heard it and knew it, and thereby transmitted it to Nanyue.
△ Third, listing the direct lineage of the patriarchs, in two parts; first, the explicit clarification, in five parts; first, the ancestral succession of Nanyue.
Nanyue successfully realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and attained the purity of the six sense faculties, transmitting it to Tiantai.
The Master, upon reading the *Sūtra on the Sublime Samādhi*, saw its praises of meditative concentration;

he subsequently sought out various masters of Chan to study Mahāyāna, frequently dwelling in forests and wilds to practice walking meditation and dhyāna. Later, he visited Master Wen to inquire about and receive the oral instructions and transmissions.
Using the method of observing the mind, he busied himself with monastic affairs by day and practiced seated meditation by night until dawn.
After twenty-one days had passed, he first attained a slight degree of stillness and observed the signs of the good and evil karma of his entire life.

As he redoubled his diligent effort, a sudden obstacle to meditation arose: his four limbs became limp and weak, and his body would not obey his mind. He then examined himself, thinking, "I am now ill."
"All arise from karma; karma originates in the mind. Fundamentally there are no external objects, yet one instead perceives the source of the mind.

Since karma cannot be grasped, one subsequently moves through the eight tactile sensations and triggers fundamental dhyāna. Because of seeing the traces of the path practiced during three lifetimes, at the end of the summer retreat, when receiving the *pravāraṇā* and about to ascend the hall, he sighed in lamentation:
'In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, after ninety days were completed, [he attained] realization...'"
"The Way is vast, yet I have now received the Dharma in vain for many years; my shame is profound.

He then leaned his body against a wall and attained a sudden, great awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. From that time forward, he understood all sutras he had not previously heard without doubt.
(From the *Tongji*). △ Second, the Patriarchal Succession of Tiantai.
At Mount Ling of Tiantai, he personally received the Great Awakening and attained wondrous enlightenment;

because his realization arose from stillness and was not dependent on others, he employed the wondrous purport of the *Lotus Sūtra* to perfect the "Three Thousand Worlds in a Single Moment" as an absolute and wondrous contemplation, which he transmitted to Zhangan.
In the first year of the Tianjia era of Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty, when Master Si was residing at Mount Dasu in Guangzhou, the Master went there to pay his respects.
Master Si said, "In the past, we listened to the Lotus Sūtra together on Vulture Peak; pursued by our karmic affinity from that time, you have come here again today.
He then showed him the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded for him the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss throughout the day and night.

He burned juniper with such intense devotion that the juniper was exhausted; he followed it with chestnut wood. He rolled up the curtains and advanced toward the moon, which had already set; he burned pine wood as an offering.
After twenty-one days, his recitation of the sutras reached the point of "True Diligence" (*bhūta-vīrya*). This is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.
His body and mind suddenly became clear and tranquil, and he entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*); from this stillness, he gave rise to illuminating insight.
The *Lotus Sūtra* was like the high radiance descending upon a secluded valley, and his realization of the characteristics of all phenomena was like a long wind wandering through the great void.
He was about to verify what he had realized from Master Bai at Mount Nanyue when [Huiyuan] further expounded it for him.

Whatever he himself had awakened to and whatever he had received through inquiry from his teacher, he practiced with even greater intensity for four nights, surpassing a hundred years of effort. Mount Nanyue sighed and said: "Were it not for you, this would not have been realized; were it not for you, this would not have been attained."
"I do not know the samādhi into which you have entered; it is the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvayoga*) of the Lotus Samādhi.
As for the dhāraṇī you have brought forth and maintained, it is the 'First Turning' (*prathama-pradakṣiṇa*) dhāraṇī.

Even if there were thousands or tens of thousands of masters of letters, your eloquence could never be exhausted. You shall be the foremost among all those who preach the Dharma. (Tongji) △ Chapter Three.
Anzucheng succeeded him.
Chang’an compiled the Dharma-treasury and transmitted it to the two Wei masters.
At the age of seven, he entered Cejing Temple to rely upon Huiji; he could memorize ten thousand words a day, and at twenty, he received full ordination.

Jietian was naturally gifted with wisdom and understanding; upon hearing something once, he never forgot it. During the Zhizhide era, he first visited Zhiyi at Xuchan Temple to receive instruction in the methods of contemplation (*guanfa*).
After long and diligent study, he suddenly received Zhiyi’s seal of approval and became his attendant.
Wherever they stayed, he was able to fully comprehend every Dharma gate that was preached. In the first year of the Zhengming era, he accompanied Zhiyi to reside at Jinshan.

Ling Guangzhai listened to lectures on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In the summer of the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he received the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) at Yuyuan in Jiangling;
in the summer of the fourteenth year, he received the *Yuandun zhiguan* (Complete and Sudden Calming and Contemplation) at Yuyuan.
As for the sequence of his lectures and studies at other locations, they were all compiled into more than one hundred sections of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures.
That the various teachings previously unheard have been transmitted is entirely due to the Master’s merit; thus, the panegyrist says:
"In the past, when the Wise One (Zhezhì) was sent by the Buddha to personally hear the purport of the *Lotus Sūtra* at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he bestowed it upon China.

He then established the Eight Teachings and employed the Three Contemplations and Four Modes of Discernment to proclaim the Dharma for those with the appropriate capacity. This may indeed be said. As for its transmission in this final age..."
As for the transmission of this [teaching], Zhiyi entrusted it to Zhizhe, who relied upon the right side of the Master;

with his talent for universal memorization and his skillful brush, he composed commentaries and treatises to be passed down to future generations. His merit and virtue are truly comparable to those of Ānanda at the First Council.
Had it not been for Zhizhe, I fear that the Way of Zhiyi would have ceased to be heard in our own day (from the *Tongji*). △ Fourth, the ancestral succession of the Three Masters.
Wei transmitted [the Dharma] to Zuoxi; Zuoxi transmitted it to Jingxi.

After the Venerable Fahu (Zhiyi) had entered the service of Zhang’an as his teacher and received full ordination, he inquired after and received the essentials of the mind, whereby both concentration and wisdom were simultaneously awakened, and he immediately realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.
In the first year of the Shangyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he went to Xuan-yuan Lian-dan Mountain.

By day he lectured and by night he practiced meditation, while transcribing the Tripitaka scriptures with his own hand; thus, he named that place "Fahua" (Lotus). Subsequently, students flocked there:
three hundred people practiced meditation, and the assembly of those listening to lectures numbered seven hundred. They were regularly divided into nine locations for the summer retreat.
